articles.title: In latest blow to Obamacare, Trump is threatening the entire US health system
articles.summary: The Trump administration is removing 760,000 people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act marketplace
articles.body:
The Trump administration is removing 760,000 people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace on allegations of fraud, officials said on Tuesday – adding to previous efforts to chip away at federally subsidized insurance programs and likely causing some of the lowest-income Americans to forego healthcare, experts said.

The US government is also investigating about 420,000 people whom they suspect of fraud, and they are putting a six-month enrollment moratorium on new agents and brokers selling Obamacare policies, officials said at a press conference.

The removed enrollees are a mixture of "phantoms" and "ghosts" as well as people who don't meet the eligibility requirements of Obamacare, said Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).

"These are not real people," he said, claiming that expelling them from the ACA marketplace would save the federal government $2.2bn.

JD Vance, who is leading a federal taskforce on fraud, claimed: "We're actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them."

No details were provided about how many enrollees were fictional, enrolled by fraudulent brokers without their knowledge or expelled because of income restrictions.

"There's no transparency about who these people are and why they're being disenrolled, but I think it's a reasonable concern that some number are being disenrolled inappropriately," said Edwin Park, a research professor at the Center for Children and Families at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy. "A common theme here is to make it incredibly burdensome for individuals to enroll and stay enrolled in their health coverage."

Without more information, "there is no way to know how many legitimately enrolled people had their plans canceled", said Cynthia Cox, senior vice-president and director of the Program on the ACA at KFF, an independent health policy organization.

The move follows recent rules and legislation to reduce enrollment in Medicaid, Medicare and the ACA, said Park, who added: "A lot of these actions are intended to sharply undercut the success of and the long-term viability of the ACA's coverage expansions, which have been an incredible success in terms of reducing the number of people without health insurance."

About 19.2 million Americans are enrolled in the ACA marketplace, but nearly 3 million people lost their coverage between February 2025 and February 2026, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.

The fraud taskforce has also withheld $2.2bn in Medicaid payments from California and Minnesota over alleged fraud – primarily in home health aide programs, which disability advocates say are a lifeline .

Officials followed an unusual path to verify ACA enrollment, experts said. The administration sent to insurers a list of more than a million people suspected of being fraudulently enrolled in the ACA marketplace, also known as Obamacare. Officials said on Tuesday that they used AI tools to identify the enrollees.

The people were identified by three factors: they'd been enrolled by a broker or agent, had all of their ACA premium paid by the tax credit, and they had not supplied social security numbers or immigration documents.

Insurers were asked to try to make contact with those enrollees; they were permitted to filter out people who had a previous claim or had communicated with the insurer. The enrollees had 30 days to respond, or their coverage was canceled.

"It is entirely possible that many of these people were enrolled without their knowledge or were so-called phantom enrollees," Cox said. "It is also entirely possible that many of these people were legitimately enrolled and simply did not respond in time."

People can appeal and be reinstated once they prove their identities – but this will likely function as an additional hurdle making it harder for people to stay enrolled, Park said.

"We know that when you add a lot of red tape, increase the amount of complexity and the requirements for paperwork," Park said, that "leads to eligible people being disenrolled."

Vance spoke of two fraudulent brokers who were convicted of quietly enrolling people to collect commissions from insurance companies, acknowledging that "some of those people were probably legitimate", but he did not speak of the steps necessary to reinstate them or to prevent future disenrollments.

Ending unscrupulous broker practices has been a bipartisan issue , and the Biden administration was the first to act, finalizing a rule to crack down on shady brokers. Officials under Biden decertified about 200 such brokers – but Trump administration officials recertified them last year.

About 35% of ACA enrollees have never used their health insurance, Oz said. "That's just not possible," he said, adding, "So we know there is fraud."

But it's not unusual for healthy people to be enrolled in insurance and not need to use it, Park noted: "You can expect in any insurance risk pool that there's going to be a lot of people who don't use much healthcare or use healthcare at all." By removing lower-risk enrollees, insurance premiums could increase or insurers could decide to leave markets entirely, he said.

Some enrollees also appear to have been cut because they are low-income. The Affordable Care Act was intended to include a Medicaid expansion for those living under the poverty line, but a supreme court decision made the expansion optional. In states that chose not to expand Medicaid, there is a group of low-income people who make too much money to qualify for Medicaid – earning between $16,000 and $22,000 per year – but don't make enough to qualify for the ACA.

"We're going to make sure that they actually meet the income threshold requirements in order to receive these Obamacare benefits," Vance said of this group. Oz called their disenrollment "a little bit painful".

Park said that there have been a series of "at best misleading" allegations arguing that a large share of current marketplace plan enrollees are fraudulently or inappropriately enrolled. Reports from the Paragon Institute and the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) have indicated millions of fraudulent enrollees – but those analyses are "flawed", Park said.

These reports directly compare administrative data and unadjusted census data, but income and household sizes are calculated differently in these two measures. The census counts all individuals living in the household, while Medicaid and the ACA marketplace exclude non-dependent relatives.

"That has a big effect on the number of people who appear to be in certain income ranges," Park said. "That has been used to say a huge percent of people don't look like they have incomes in the right eligibility range."

These disenrollments are happening in the context of major cuts to the marketplace. Premiums skyrocketed, doubling or tripling for some enrollees, after Republicans opposed extending the enhanced tax credits at the end of last year. Alongside other financial pressures, like higher energy and food costs, "there's going to be an increasing number of people who can no longer afford their share of the premium", Park said.

The healthcare cuts of the budget reconciliation law HR1 "in many ways were designed to undermine the Affordable Care Act coverage expansions" without explicitly repealing it – a longtime Trump promise, Park said.

The Trump administration has also created new regulations to restrict marketplace enrollment, he noted, adding: "You add it all together, and you're going to have certainly significant reductions in enrollment – with those enrollment losses increasing over time."

When people lose their health insurance, it has ripple effects – including added pressure on health systems that affect all patients.

"Providers, particularly safety net providers, operate under thinner operating margins. If they're facing payment cuts, they're facing higher uncompensated care costs, as a result of more uninsured [patients]," Park said, which may lead hospitals to cut services or staff, or close their doors entirely. "And that makes it harder for everyone to access the care they need."

articles.title: Manchin: ‘If character means anything, you can’t vote for Ken Paxton’
articles.summary: Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) on Sunday took aim at Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate in the Lone Star State’s Senate race, der...
articles.body:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) on Sunday took aim at Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate in the Lone Star State's Senate race, deriding his "character."

During an interview with NewsNation's Chris Stirewalt on "The Hill Sunday," Manchin was asked about Texas's Democratic Senate candidate, state Rep. James Talarico.

"I don't know that young man, and things he's said I'm discouraged about, but I can tell you, if character means anything, you can't vote for Ken Paxton, if character means anything, because he has none," Manchin said. "So, you have a situation there."

While Democrats usually face electoral struggles in the Lone Star State, Paxton comes with notable baggage. He previously faced impeachment in the Texas House on corruption charges before he was later acquitted by the state's Senate three years ago.

In a recent poll, Talarico had a slight lead over Paxton. The NBC 5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group survey found that 46 percent of registered voters supported Talarico, while 43 percent backed Paxton.

The national political environment has also been recently rough for the GOP, with President Trump's approval rating recently slumping, the unpopular war in Iran nearing the seven-month mark, widespread concerns about the cost of living, and Republicans falling behind Democrats on key issues like immigration and healthcare in recent polling.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump's approval rating on Sunday evening was sitting at 38.8 percent , with his disapproval rating at 59.6 percent.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Texas Senate race as a "toss-up."

The Hill has reached out to Paxton's campaign for comment.

articles.title: Quaest: Lula avança entre mulheres, baixa renda e católicos | G1
articles.standfirst: Na comparação com a semana anterior, Lula passou de 37% para 40% entre mulheres e de 43% para 48% entre católicos. Recortes são da disputa de 1º turno.
articles.summary: Na comparação com a semana anterior, Lula passou de 37% para 40% entre mulheres e de 43% para 48% entre católicos. Recortes são da disputa de 1º turno.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta segunda-feira (28) mostra que Lula (PT) avançou numericamente nas intenções de voto para o primeiro turno entre mulheres, eleitores de menor renda, beneficiários do Bolsa Família e católicos, na comparação com o levantamento de 21 de setembro.

Nos quatro grupos, o presidente aparece à frente de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). O maior aumento numérico de Lula nesses recortes foi entre católicos: de 43% para 48%.

🔎 Entre mulheres, o petista passou de 37% para 40%. Na faixa de renda familiar de até dois salários mínimos, foi de 49% para 52%. Entre beneficiários do Bolsa Família, oscilou um ponto, de 52% para 53%.

As margens de erro desses recortes variam de três pontos percentuais entre mulheres e católicos, quatro entre eleitores com renda familiar de até dois salários mínimos e cinco entre beneficiários do Bolsa Família, sempre para mais ou para menos.

Encomendada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo, a pesquisa ouviu 2.004 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, em entrevistas domiciliares presenciais, entre 24 e 27 de setembro. A margem de erro para o total da amostra é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%.

O levantamento foi registrado no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) sob o número BR-06520/2026.

Quaest: cenários de 1º turno em que Lula tem vantagem — Foto: Arte/g1

Mulheres, eleitores de menor renda e escolaridade

Entre as mulheres , Lula tinha 37% nas duas pesquisas anteriores, divulgadas em 14 e 21 de setembro, e agora aparece com 40%. Flávio Bolsonaro passou de 32% para 29% na última semana.

Com os movimentos, a distância numérica entre os dois nesse grupo passou de cinco para 11 pontos percentuais.

Veja a comparação entre 21 e 28 de setembro:

A margem de erro do recorte é de três pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.

Entre os homens , o movimento foi diferente: Lula passou de 39% para 37%, enquanto Flávio foi de 34% para 39%. Os dois estão tecnicamente empatados nesse grupo, cuja margem de erro também é de três pontos.

Na faixa de renda familiar de até dois salários mínimos , Lula passou de 49% para 52%, e Flávio permaneceu com 23%. A distância entre eles foi de 26 para 29 pontos.

A margem de erro do recorte é quatro pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.

Nas outras faixas de renda, Lula também oscilou um ponto para cima. Entre eleitores com renda familiar de mais de dois a cinco salários mínimos, passou de 34% para 35%, enquanto Flávio foi de 33% para 36%.

Entre os que têm renda familiar superior a cinco salários mínimos , Lula passou de 29% para 30%, e Flávio, de 41% para 42%.

No recorte por escolaridade , Lula passou de 47% para 51% entre eleitores com ensino fundamental, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro foi de 27% para 25%.

Com isso, a distância entre os dois aumentou de 20 para 26 pontos percentuais na comparação com a semana anterior. A margem de erro nesse grupo é de três pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.

Entre beneficiários do Bolsa Família , Lula oscilou de 52% para 53%, enquanto Flávio passou de 23% para 21%. A diferença numérica entre os dois aumentou de 29 para 32 pontos percentuais.

Margem de erro do recorte é de cinco pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.

Entre os que não recebem o benefício , Lula passou de 32% para 35%, e Flávio permaneceu com 36%. Nesse grupo, os dois estão em empate técnico, considerando a margem de erro de dois pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos.

No recorte por religião , Lula passou de 43% para 48% entre católicos . Flávio também avançou numericamente, de 27% para 29%. A distância entre os dois aumentou de 16 para 19 pontos.

Neste segmento, a margem de erro é de três pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.

Lula também avançou numericamente entre evangélicos , de 23% para 27%, enquanto Flávio passou de 49% para 46%. O candidato do PL permanece à frente nesse grupo, mas a distância diminuiu de 26 para 19 pontos. A margem de erro do recorte é de quatro pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos.

No total da amostra, Lula tem 39% das intenções de voto no primeiro turno, ante 37% na semana anterior. Flávio Bolsonaro aparece com 34%, contra 33% no levantamento passado.

articles.title: Ricardo Salles desiste de concorrer ao Senado e declara apoio a Derrite e André do Prado | G1
articles.standfirst: O anúncio foi feito ao lado do governador Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), candidato à reeleição ao governo de São Paulo.
articles.summary: O anúncio foi feito ao lado do governador Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), candidato à reeleição ao governo de São Paulo.
articles.body:
Deputado federal Ricardo Salles — Foto: Murilo Corazza/g1

Na reta final da eleição, o candidato ao Senado por São Paulo Ricardo Salles ( Novo ) desistiu nesta segunda-feira (28) de disputar uma das duas vagas ao Senado e declarou apoio aos adversários Guilherme Derrite (PP) e André do Prado (PL).

O anúncio foi feito ao lado do governador Tarcísio de Freitas ( Republicanos ), candidato à reeleição ao governo de São Paulo. Desde o início da campanha, Salles travou uma disputa com André do Prado e o acusou de dividir o eleitorado conservador no estado.

Ao explicar a decisão, Salles afirmou que as diferenças entre os candidatos precisam ser deixadas de lado diante do que chamou de um risco de uma nova eleição do presidente Lula (PT).

"Nós estamos diante de um momento muito difícil para o país, um risco enorme de nós continuarmos nesse projeto extremamente equivocado, que está nos levando para o buraco", explicou.

Segundo Salles, em São Paulo, a liderança de Tarcísio deixa o grupo "relativamente confortável" na disputa pelo governo estadual. Ele também afirmou que é necessário "dar sinais para a sociedade" de união diante do cenário nacional.

"É importante dar sinais para a sociedade, para a gente entender que o momento é tão grave que diferenças, opiniões diferentes, têm que ser deixadas de lado, justamente porque o risco de uma catástrofe numa reeleição do presidente Lula é muito grande e o país não merece isso", disse.

Tarcísio afirmou que Salles tinha legitimidade para continuar na disputa, mas decidiu abrir mão da candidatura para contribuir com um "projeto maior".

"A gente tem o Ricardo Salles, que tinha toda a legitimidade para continuar na sua caminhada, tem trajetória, tem bagagem, tem história, dando um passo ao lado para nos ajudar, para somar. Então esse momento é o momento de somar, não é o momento de dividir", afirmou Tarcísio.

Segundo o governador, a união em torno de Derrite e Prado tem como objetivo ampliar as chances de eleger dois representantes de São Paulo para o Senado.

"É o momento da gente pensar um objetivo maior, que é vencer as eleições, que é ter dois representantes no Senado, que é entender o papel que o Senado vai ter, o papel moderador, o papel de reestabelecer aquela missão de funcionar com o sistema de freios e contrapesos. Um papel que hoje foi perdido e a gente precisa realmente revigorar. E para isso nós precisamos da melhor representação."

articles.title: Eleição entra na reta final com STF e TSE em choque | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministros do Supremo têm revisto decisões da Justiça Eleitoral, e integrantes do TSE veem tentativa de interferência na condução do pleito. Fachin busca mediar o conflito.
articles.summary: Ministros do Supremo têm revisto decisões da Justiça Eleitoral, e integrantes do TSE veem tentativa de interferência na condução do pleito. Fachin busca mediar o conflito.
articles.body:
Nunes Marques durante julgamento sobre supostas mensagens de Vorcaro para Moraes — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

A última semana antes do primeiro turno começa com uma tensão adicional no Judiciário: a disputa entre grupos do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) e do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) entrou de vez na eleição. Integrantes do Judiciário ouvidos pelo blog avaliam que o embate deve dominar os bastidores até domingo.

🔎 De um lado, ministros do Supremo vêm revendo decisões da Justiça Eleitoral e classificando, reservadamente, algumas delas como “derrapadas” do TSE.

👀 Do outro, integrantes da cúpula do tribunal eleitoral, comandado por Kassio Nunes Marques , enxergam nessas intervenções uma tentativa de retomar o protagonismo do grupo de Alexandre de Moraes na condução do pleito.

A decisão de Flávio Dino neste fim de semana tornou a tensão ainda mais explícita. Dino invalidou uma decisão de André Mendonça no TSE envolvendo publicações sobre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Nossa Senhora Aparecida, acrescentando um capítulo à disputa que já atravessava o Supremo.

O conflito, porém, vai além desse caso e já ganhou uma leitura eleitoral nas campanhas. No entorno das candidaturas, o grupo de Moraes é visto como mais favorável aos interesses de Lula (PT), enquanto a cúpula do TSE, presidida por Kassio e com Mendonça na vice-presidência, é vista como mais favorável aos interesses de Flávio Bolsonaro.

São avaliações políticas das campanhas sobre a atuação dos ministros. E ajudam a explicar por que cada decisão nesta semana tende a ser interpretada também pela lente da disputa eleitoral.

Os atritos entre STF e TSE não começaram agora. Já havia divergências sobre temas centrais desta eleição. A diferença é que o pleito chega à semana decisiva sem o alinhamento institucional que marcou outros momentos da relação entre as cortes.

Na eleição passada, havia uma interlocução afinada entre Rosa Weber, então presidente do Supremo, e Alexandre de Moraes, que comandava o TSE. Hoje, essa articulação não se repete.

Edson Fachin preside o Supremo e tenta exercer um papel de mediação, mas encontra uma Corte fragmentada e atravessada pela crise do caso Master. Moraes, Dino e Gilmar Mendes têm peso próprio no tribunal. Kassio e Mendonça, que comandam a Justiça Eleitoral, estão do outro lado de algumas das principais disputas internas do STF.

Apesar das divergências, os grupos compartilham uma queixa: a falta de comando de Fachin na Corte.

O presidente do Supremo chamou os ministros para conversar e tentar baixar a temperatura. No grupo de Moraes, porém, a avaliação é que Fachin tem margem limitada para interferir na atuação individual dos colegas. O argumento é que, se um processo chega ao STF e um ministro entende que uma decisão do TSE afronta direitos ou a jurisprudência da Corte, não caberia ao presidente impedir essa atuação.

É nesse ponto que a tensão pode se renovar ao longo da semana: cada decisão relevante do TSE pode abrir uma nova batalha no Supremo. Kassio e Mendonça decidem na Justiça Eleitoral; partidos e candidatos recorrem; e ministros do STF, quando provocados, podem rever essas decisões.

Para integrantes do Judiciário ouvidos pelo blog , a disputa vai além de quem ganha ou perde em cada processo. O que está em jogo é quem dará a última palavra sobre os conflitos eleitorais até domingo.

articles.summary: Pesquisa encomendada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo ouviu 2.004 pessoas entre 24 e 27 de setembro.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta segunda-feira (28) mostra que Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) estão empatados no cenário de 2º turno, ambos com 42% das intenções de voto .

O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo.

Flávio mantém 42% de intenções de voto pela terceira rodada consecutiva. Lula tinha 40% há duas semanas, depois oscilou para 41% e agora tem 42%.

A Quaest ouviu 2.004 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 24 e 27 de setembro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa é BR-06520/2026.

articles.title: Pesquisa Quaest presidente: Felipe Nunes analisa Lula e Flávio | G1
articles.standfirst: Diretor da Quaest e professor da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV), Felipe Nunes avalia momento atual da corrida pelo Palácio do Planalto.
articles.summary: O cientista político Felipe Nunes detalha como a Pesquisa Quaest mostra a recuperação de Lula entre mulheres e o empate técnico com Flávio na disputa presidencial.
articles.body:
1. Com redução de indecisos (10% -> 5%) e voto útil (16% -> 12%) nos últimos 15 dias, Lula começa a última semana do 1º turno na liderança com 39%. Flávio chega a 34%. Cury e Caiado tem 4% cada, empatados com Renan, que tem 3% e Zema com 1%.

Veja a análise da pesquisa Quaest para presidente de 28 de setembro — Foto: Reprodução/Quaest

2. Lula e Flávio voltam a ficar numericamente empatados na simulação de 2º turno: 42 x 42. Flávio se mantém nos 42% nas últimas três rodadas. Lula oscilou +2 pontos no mesmo período. Indecisos são 3% e 13% não vão votar em ninguém.

3. A recuperação de terreno de Lula aconteceu de forma mais clara em 3 subgrupos: entre as mulheres. O que era um empate duas semanas atrás, virou uma vantagem de +9 pp em favor de Lula.

4. Lula também abriu mais vantagem sobre Flávio entre eleitores de baixa renda. O incumbente tem aparece com uma vantagem de +26 pp sobre Flávio.

5. A mesma tendência observada entre os beneficiários do Bolsa Família. Neste segmento, Lula voltou a ter 59% das intenções de voto, contra 27% de Flávio.

6. O aumento da vantagem entre mulheres, eleitores de baixa renda e beneficiários do BF parece estar muito associado ao pacote de medidas anunciado pelo governo na última semana. A restrição às bets é aprovada por 62%, o reajuste do Bolsa Família por 59% e a distribuição das canetas emagrecedoras no SUS por 58%.

7. As mulheres são as que mais aprovam as medidas: 64% delas aprovam proibição às bets, e 62% aprovam tanto as canetinhas no SUS quanto o reajuste do Bolsa Família.

8. O eleitor de baixa renda é o que mais aprova as canetinhas emagrecedoras e o reajuste do Bolsa. Mas chama atenção que a proibição às bets fura a bolha e é ainda mais aprovada por quem tem renda mais alta.

9. Também houve uma leve recuperação entre católicos. Lula aparece com +13 pp a frente de Flávio neste sub-grupo, o melhor resultado do presidente nesse segmento desde 14/ago. Entre evangélicos, a vantagem de Flávio diminuiu.

10. O questionário já havia sido registrado no TSE quando a polêmica envolvendo N.S. Aparecida foi iniciado nas redes. Mas há forte evidência que o tema favoreceu Lula ao aumentar o medo da volta da família Bolsonaro entre católicos.

11. O medo da volta da família Bolsonaro a Presidência também cresceu entre mulheres. Enquanto o medo de Lula continuar no poder crescer entre os homens. Ou seja, o Gap de gênero aumentou nessa reta final de 1º turno.

12. Outra boa notícia para o governo é a melhora relativa na aprovação do governo. Semana passada o saldo negativo do governo era de -6 pp, agora esse saldo negativo caiu para -3 pp. Lula volta a ter probabilidade acima de 50% de reeleição.

13. A probabilidade de reeleição só não é maior porque Lula continua tendo um saldo negativo de avaliação (-7 pp.). Nenhum presidente foi capaz de vencer eleição no Brasil com saldo negativo a essa altura da corrida presidencial.

14. O efeito positivo sobre aprovação do governo também fez oscilar positivamente o potencial de voto de Lula (de 45% para 46%) e oscilar pra baixo a rejeição (de 55% para 54%). Flávio mantém seu potencial de voto em 43% e sua rejeição em 56%.

15. A Quaest entrevistou 2.004 pessoas, entre os dias 24 e 27/set; a margem de erro é de 2pp e o nível de confiabilidade de 95%. Registro no TSE: BR-6520/2026.

articles.title: TRE-PI suspende propaganda de Tiago Junqueira por erro na votação | G1
articles.standfirst: Propaganda dizia para eleitor votar duas vezes no número do candidato, o que, conforme o art. 206, § 2º, da Resolução TSE nº 23.751/2026, anula um dos votos. Ao g1, o candidato informou que a intenção era pedir votos na primeira ou segunda opção e que reformulará vídeo para melhor entendimento do eleitor.
articles.summary: Tiago Junqueira teve propaganda suspensa pelo TRE-PI por orientar o voto duplo para o Senado, prática que resulta na anulação da escolha conforme as regras eleitorais.
articles.body:
TRE-PI proíbe propaganda do candidato ao senado Tiago Junqueira (PL) por induzir eleitor a anular voto — Foto: g1 PI

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Piauí (TRE-PI) determinou a suspensão da veiculação de propaganda do candidato ao Senado pelo Piauí Tiago Junqueira (PL). A decisão é de domingo (27), e motivada porque, conforme o Juiz Federal Rodrigo Pinheiro do Nascimento, a propaganda induz o eleitor ao erro ao orientar o voto duas vezes no número do candidato, o que anula o segundo voto .

Ao g1 , o candidato informou que a intenção era pedir votos na primeira ou segunda opção e que reformulará vídeo para melhor entendimento do eleitor.

Na propaganda veiculada pela campanha, o candidato pede que o eleitor vote duas vezes no número dele para as duas vagas do Senado. A decisão diz que o candidato e a coligação têm 24 horas, contado da intimação, para suspender a reapresentação do vídeo.

➡️Entenda: o Senado tem 81 cadeiras, e o mandato dos senadores é de oito anos. A renovação acontece de forma alternada: em uma eleição são escolhidos dois senadores por estado e pelo Distrito Federal, renovando dois terços da Casa. Na eleição seguinte, apenas uma vaga por unidade da Federação é disputada.

Está determinada a suspensão "[...] no horário eleitoral gratuito, em blocos ou inserções de rádio e televisão, bem como via internet, a peça publicitária identificada no ID 22705473, bem como de reproduzir a orientação de que o eleitor pode atribuir dois votos válidos para o Senado Federal ao mesmo candidato, inclusive mediante simulação do funcionamento da urna eletrônica", determina o juiz.

O magistrado fixou ainda multa coercitiva de R$ 5 mil a cada veiculação que ocorra descumprindo a decisão após o término do prazo.

Ele determinou também a comunicação às emissoras de TV e rádio responsáveis pela geração do horário eleitoral gratuito no Estado do Piauí para adoção de providências quanto à peça publicitária.

Para o voto correto , a urna eletrônica pedirá o voto para senador duas vezes. Primeiro, o eleitor digita o número do candidato, confere a foto e confirma. Em seguida, a urna abre uma segunda tela para que seja escolhido outro candidato ao Senado.

articles.title: Disputa Flávio Dino x André Mendonça mostra como crise no STF afeta as eleições | G1
articles.body:
O presidente do STF , Edson Fachin, recebe na manhã desta segunda-feira (28) os ministros Kassio Nunes Marques, André Mendonça e Dias Toffoli, que integram a composição titular da Corte Eleitoral.

A reunião será fechada e não deve constar da agenda oficial. A conversa ocorre em meio à crise entre ministros do STF e à preocupação com possíveis reflexos no TSE às vésperas da eleição.

Nos bastidores, uma avaliação é de que aliados do ministro Alexandre de Moraes estariam tentando levar a crise do Supremo para o Tribunal Eleitoral. Segundo essa leitura, o movimento teria começado após uma manifestação pública de Gilmar Mendes sobre a atuação do TSE e o papel da Corte no processo eleitoral.

No último fim de semana, depois do ministro Mendonça mandar retirar do ar um post do colunista Antônio Tabet, no qual ele trata da polêmica sobre um projeto para tirar de Nossa Senhora Aparecida o título de padroeira do Brasil, o ministro Flávio Dino foi acionado e derrubou a decisão do colega.

Os dois já estão em campos opostos na crise do STF. Mendonça querendo investigar Alexandre de Moraes. Flávio Dino defendendo que todos sejam investigados.

Agora, Dino diz que a decisão de Mendonça fere a liberdade de eleitores cobrarem de candidatos suas posições políticas. E mandou avisar que outros atingidos podem também pedir a extensão da medida.

A entidade rebateu e disse que mentira não se combate com mentira. O conflito atinge eleitores católicos mais intensamente do que evangelicos.

Em relação à decisão de Flávio Dino derrubando a de Mendonça, ele disse que o humorista Antônio Tebet não chegou a citar o nome de Flávio Bolsonaro. Disse: "A família miliciana odeia tanto mulher preta que resolver atacar Nossa Senhora Aparecida". Uma referência nem muito indireta aos Bolsonaro.

Ministro do STF Flávio Dino, André Mendonça e Alexandre de Moraes — Foto: Gustavo Moreno/STF

A decisão de Dino marca também um confronto entre STF e TSE. A defesa de Flávio Bolsonaro criticou a intromissão do Supremo num tema afeto ao TSE . Mas não foi a primeira.

Antes, Gilmar Mendes decidiu que o reajuste do Bolsa Família não afeta legislação eleitoral, antecipando-se a uma decisão do ministro André Mendonça sobre uma ação do partido Novo contra o reajuste.

Outro ponto de atrito entre os dois tribunais foi quando Alexandre de Moraes decidiu pedir explicações ao PL e Flávio Bolsonaro sobre o uso de inteligência artificial com Bolsonaro na convenção do partido.

Antecipou-se a uma resposta do relator do caso no TSE, o presidente Nunes Marques. Em meio a tudo isso, o ministro Gilmar Mendes chegou a mandar um alerta para que ministros do TSE, num recado direto aos indicados por Bolsonaro Nunes Marques e André Mendonça, não tomassem decisões políticas. Ameaçando inclusive com a atuação do STF como casa revisora do TSE.

articles.title: Lula aposta em pacote de bondades, e Flávio Bolsonaro busca 'voto útil' na reta final a disputa presidencial | G1
articles.body:
Na reta final antes do primeiro turno, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), candidato à reeleição, partiu para o ataque: anunciou o reajuste do Bolsa Família, prometeu canetas emagrecedoras no SUS e decretou o fim das bets , medidas que visam o eleitorado feminino e evangélico.

O principal adversário dele nas urnas, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), aposta no voto útil nesta reta final, contando com a migração de votos de Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Augusto Cury (Avante) e Romeu Zema (Novo) para ele ganhar a eleição no primeiro turno.

Há um grande contingente de eleitores indecisos, principalmente mulheres e eleitores no Sudeste e no Sul.

É esse grupo que está em disputa nesta última semana de campanha. Com os dois líderes chegando empatados na reta final.

O diretor da Quaest, Felipe Nunes, destaca que, apesar da estabilidade do resultado consolidado das pesquisas, há movimentações de votos por dentro dos levantamentos. Quem conseguir ter a melhor mensagem irá chegar na frente na disputa do primeiro turno.

Além dessa disputa, Felipe Nunes ressalta como último fator decisório da câmara já será o debate da TV Globo na quinta-feira (1º).

Depois de Flávio Bolsonaro garantir que estará no debate da Globo, a equipe de Lula diz ainda não haver uma decisão se ele irá. Mas a presença do adversário deve forçá-lo a participar.

Vai ser o primeiro confronto entre os dois até aqui na eleição. Será muito provavelmente o fator que irá definir o voto dos eleitores indecisos nesta reta final da campanha.

articles.title: Sen Kennedy says no living politicians should have buildings named after them after Trump's moves
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy has proposed barring living politicians from having buildings named after them as Trump pushes to rename the Kennedy Center.
articles.body: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Sunday that living public officials should not have buildings named after them and proposed a rule to prohibit such renaming efforts. This comes as President Donald Trump continues to push to rename the Kennedy Center after himself. The president has also sought to rename other prominent federal buildings in Washington, D.C., after himself since returning to the White House last year. Kennedy said public officials, including Trump, should not "spend public money on private ads for themselves." "The White House sees it differently, but … you can’t spend public money to … promote yourself," Kennedy told host Margaret Brennan during an appearance on CBS News' "Face the Nation." KENNEDY CENTER CEILING PARTIALLY COLLAPSES AS TRUMP-LED BOARD PUSHES FOR 2-YEAR CLOSURE Kennedy's comments came as a new ad promoting Trump appeared on multiple networks that was funded by the federal government. The senator then suggested public officials should be barred from having a building named after them while they are still alive. "I may end up with a sombrero on my head, but I also think we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him when he’s alive," he said, referring to Trump mocking Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., last year by sharing AI videos of the lawmakers wearing sombreros. FEDERAL JUDGE ORDERS TRUMP'S NAME REMOVED FROM KENNEDY CENTER, SAYS ONLY CONGRESS CAN RENAME IT Trump has attempted to rename multiple buildings after himself since returning to the Oval Office, including the Kennedy Center, although federal judges blocked multiple attempts by the center's board — handpicked by Trump — to add the president’s name to the building. Trump's name was briefly added to the building's facade but was ordered removed after courts ruled that only Congress holds the authority to change the center's name. The State Department also added Trump’s name last year to the U.S. Institute of Peace, but former institute officials removed by the Trump administration filed a court motion earlier this month to block construction crews from putting the president’s name onto the outside of the building. Trump also suggested he wanted New York's Penn Station and the D.C.-area's Dulles Airport named after him as a condition for a funding deal earlier this year. The president has additionally floated a project to construct a promenade connecting the back of the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River, saying that allies wanted to call it the "Trump Promenade." articles.title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
articles.summary: The most revealing thing about the summit in Washington may be what the two leaders did not say - and what we still don't know.
articles.body:
On Monday, China released more information of what was agreed at the talks between Xi Jinping and Donald Tump last week, shedding light on a handful of concrete outcomes.

But there were no joint statements and few major breakthroughs.

Instead, both governments issued separate accounts of the meeting - perhaps a sign that despite the White House tours and promise of warmer ties, Washington and Beijing remain wary of each other.

Here are four things we now know - and still don't - about what transpired at the talks.

A new AI dialogue and communication channel

Beijing says it has agreed with Washington to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for the end of November.

As both countries race to develop advanced artificial intelligence, the move suggests they see a need for some guardrails around a technology that is increasingly being used in everything from business to military planning.

They have also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents, aimed at preventing misunderstandings or unexpected developments from turning into a broader confrontation.

The meeting was being closely watched for any developments or agreements in relation to AI - especially in the wake of calls by US companies like Anthropic to slow down developments, and revelations that Open AI had gained unauthorised access to government websites in countries like Australia and had "meddled" with multiple US government agency sites.

Huge data centres rise at 'China speed' to power its AI ambitions

Trump and Xi come face-to-face as US and China battle to win the AI race

Trump wants AI to be rebranded as super intelligence. Will it work?

Trade truce - what was included and what was left out

Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January.

The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year.

Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December.

It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently.

But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough.

China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing.

Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs.

The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028.

There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased.

The US left out Taiwan - but China didn't

The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping.

According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution.

After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack.

He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue.

"We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend.

"Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel."

Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months.

Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit.

The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so.

Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

China may be opening the investment doors

China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations.

The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it.

Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed.

Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen.

And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans.

Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention.

So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place.

This summit produced more dialogue - but very little decision change for now. The most contentious issues from advanced technology to Taiwan remain unresolved.

But for both leaders, this is a familiar outcome - a promise of more channels of communication, modest economic concessions and modest proposals to steady relations.

And while both remain committed to a steady relationship - continued US-China dialogue appears far easier than asking either superpower to compromise.

articles.title: France’s far-right National Rally gains ground in Senate vote
articles.summary: The vote marks the first time the far-right party gained enough seats to form its own caucus.
articles.body:
France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and its allies have secured a record 14 seats in the Senate, effectively quadrupling its number in the 348-seat chamber just months before a presidential election.

Sunday’s indirect election ⁠of senators marked the first time Marine Le Pen ’s party won enough seats to form its own caucus.

“The results have exceeded our expectations,” Le Pen, the party’s leader and presidential candidate, said in a post on X.

“This is a historic victory, and a major milestone with the formation for the first time of a group in the Senate.”

RN entered the Senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the National Front, and won three seats in 2023.

It emerged as the single largest party in the lower-house National Assembly after President Emmanuel Macron called snap polls in 2024, though it fell well short of a majority.

Le Pen is preparing to run in next year’s presidential election when centrist Macron steps down.

RN president Jordan Bardella said the party’s senators would form an alliance with the Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR).

The right, centre and left-wing Socialists looked set to remain the three major forces in the upper house, according to initial results.

articles.title: Data centers could be the sleeper issue of the 2026 midterm elections
articles.summary: Data centers may be the sleeper issue of the midterms as a Gallup survey found 70% of Americans oppose new AI facilities in their communities.
articles.body: Data centers may be the sleeper issue of the midterm elections. Fox News reported that Senate candidates are confronting growing voter anger over the electricity costs, water consumption and sprawling developments associated with artificial intelligence. One recent Gallup survey found that 70% of Americans oppose the construction of new AI data centers in their own communities. Politicians are paying attention. Some are calling for moratoriums. Others are targeting tax incentives or demanding that projects generate their own power. The political temptation is obvious: When voters are worried about higher utility bills and rapid changes in their communities, blaming large technology companies is easier than explaining a complicated energy and infrastructure problem. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER The concerns are real. They should not be dismissed by industry, and they cannot be ignored by elected officials. No family should be forced to subsidize the grid upgrades required by one of the world’s wealthiest companies. Communities deserve honest answers about water use, noise, land, electricity demand, tax incentives and who will pay for new infrastructure. But, legitimate concerns are quickly hardening into something far more dangerous: a political campaign against the physical infrastructure of American artificial intelligence. If that happens, we will repeat one of the most damaging patterns in modern American history. For decades, the United States surrendered factories, critical supply chains, mineral production and industrial capacity to foreign competitors. Communities lost jobs, our national security became dependent on adversaries, and Washington eventually spent billions trying to rebuild industries that should never have left. THE AI REVOLUTION COULD BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY DISASTER IF WE AREN'T CAREFUL We cannot make the same mistake with AI. Artificial intelligence does not exist somewhere in the cloud. It requires chips, servers, power plants, transmission lines, cooling systems, construction workers, electricians, pipefitters, engineers and data centers. These facilities are not incidental to the AI economy. They are the factories of the next industrial age. AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL China understands this. Beijing is not debating whether it should possess the energy and computing infrastructure necessary to dominate artificial intelligence. It is building. The International Energy Agency projects that data-center electricity consumption will increase substantially in both China and the United States through 2030. If America decides that data centers are too politically difficult to construct, the demand for AI will not disappear. The investment, jobs, technical expertise and strategic advantage will simply move elsewhere. That would be a profound failure of American competitiveness. It would also create a serious political problem for Democrats. Data-center construction has become an important source of work for the building trades. The Associated Press recently reported that data centers account for at least 40% of the work hours performed by members of the Columbus-Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council and at least 50% for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 26 in the Washington metropolitan area. WELDER TURNED LAWMAKER SEES A ‘NUCLEAR BOMB FOR WORK’ — AND A CHANCE TO HELP BLUE COLLAR AMERICANS Those are not theoretical jobs promised years from now. They are jobs for electricians, laborers, operating engineers, pipefitters and other skilled workers today. Democrats cannot claim to represent organized labor while allowing progressive activists to shut down the projects employing union members. Republicans should resist a similar temptation. Conservatives have spent years arguing for reshoring, energy dominance, permitting reform, American manufacturing and competition with China. Those commitments mean very little if they disappear when building the next American industry becomes locally controversial. The answer is not to wave every project through without conditions. It is to build responsibly and communicate honestly. Data-center developers should be expected to explain what they are building, how much electricity and water it will require, how they will protect residential ratepayers and what the surrounding community will receive in return. Utilities and regulators should ensure that large customers pay the costs created by their demand. Projects should pursue closed-loop cooling, on-site generation, long-term power agreements and other options that reduce pressure on local systems. TO BEAT CHINA IN AI, AMERICA MUST WORK WITH COMMUNITIES — NOT AROUND THEM Most importantly, America needs more energy. Data centers are exposing a problem that existed before the AI boom. Electricity demand from data centers has tripled over the past decade and could double or triple again by 2028. Electricity demand is rising after years of stagnant generation, premature plant retirements, congested transmission systems and permitting processes that make major infrastructure nearly impossible to build on time. Stopping data centers will not modernize the grid. Building more reliable generation, accelerating transmission, preserving existing nuclear capacity, expanding natural gas infrastructure and deploying advanced nuclear power will. Industry also needs to recognize that silence is no longer a strategy. As Sen. Jon Husted told Fox News, data-center companies have not done a good enough job explaining why they should be allowed to develop in communities. He is right. Americans hear about enormous power consumption, water use and tax incentives. They need to hear, in plain language, what data centers make possible, which jobs they create, how they support national security and why domestic computing capacity matters in the competition with China. That education must happen before a project is announced, not after opposition has already formed. Political leadership means taking voters’ concerns seriously without allowing fear to determine America’s economic future. We can protect ratepayers, demand transparency, give communities a meaningful voice and still build the infrastructure required to compete. articles.title: Right-wing conservatives push to shut down the last active Jan. 6 prosecution
articles.summary: They say Brian Cole Jr. was framed. The Justice Department is pressing forward with the case.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — There’s just one active federal prosecution still tied to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, the case of the man accused of planting two pipe bombs near the Republican National Committee and the Democratic National Committee. And some of MAGA’s most fervent supporters want to shut it down. Some conservative figures accuse the Trump administration of framing Brian Cole Jr., who was arrested almost five years after the unexploded devices were placed. Cole, as NBC News first reported, told the FBI that he believed the 2020 election had been stolen after false accusations fueled by President Donald Trump and his supporters. Cole has pleaded not guilty, and a trial is set for February. The FBI said he confessed after his arrest, but his legal team has noted that he was diagnosed with autism and is expected to seek to have the confession tossed based on his disability or argue he was coerced. The prosecution has opened a rift between the Trump administration and some prominent right-wing conservatives who are seeking to undermine the case by spreading discredited theories about who was to blame. They contend the bombs were placed by “deep state” actors to distract from the police response and make Jan. 6 seem more violent. Right-wing activists have appeared in court to support Cole, and former Jan. 6 defendants are backing him online. Trump pardoned Jan. 6 defendants as one of his first acts in office, and as a result, the Justice Department shut down ongoing investigations into the rioters who beat and bloodied law enforcement and caused an estimated $2.7 billion in costs. Legally, federal prosecutors pushed forward with the pipe bomb case because the devices were placed the night before the attack and therefore the crime wasn’t covered under Trump’s mass Jan. 6 pardon. The devices were viable but didn’t explode, law enforcement said. Culturally, it’s been a right-wing talking point for years. In a 2024 podcast, Dan Bongino said he had “zero doubt” the bombs were an inside job. When Bongino became the FBI’s deputy director, he pushed the stalled investigation forward. During the announcement of Cole’s arrest, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi credited him with helping crack the case. Bongino, who left the bureau in January, has not directly addressed how — or whether — his opinions on the “inside job” theory have changed. After the December arrest, he told Fox News commentator Sean Hannity in an interview: “I was paid in the past, Sean, for my opinions, that’s clear, and one day I will be back in that space — but that’s not what I’m paid for now.” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., publicly posted a photo of officials — including Bondi, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, FBI Director Kash Patel and Bongino — at the news conference announcing Cole’s arrest and said they were “complicit” in a conspiracy. “The evidence is mounting,” Massie said on social media. “All of the people who took credit at the podium upon the arrest of Brian Cole Jr. are complicit, either through negligence or malfeasance. Mr. Cole is not the J5/J6 pipe bomber, and the identity of the actual perpetrator is being obscured. Bookmark it.” Before Cole was arrested, the FBI questioned Shauni Kerkhoff, a former Capitol Police officer who was suggested as a possible suspect by reporters for The Blaze, a right-wing website founded by Glenn Beck, based upon a “gait analysis.” The story was co-written by former Jan. 6 defendant Steve Baker, who pleaded guilty in November 2024 to four misdemeanors but was never sentenced. Kerkhoff, who had testified in the first Jan. 6 trial, against an armed pro-Trump rioter named Guy Reffitt, was also named in a Blaze story that accused the Capitol Police of using excessive force. Her lawyers say the FBI told her they were investigating “online chatter” — a reference to The Blaze’s reporting — and subjected her to “a search of her home by caravan of armed agents, a bomb-disposal truck, and a helicopter, followed by a three-hour polygraph interrogation,” before she was eventually cleared. Kerkhoff, who now works campus security for the CIA, is not a suspect and has not been charged with a crime. The Justice Department has said the former Capitol Police officer has “become the target of a malicious online conspiracy,” and that while the FBI investigated her, it found the claims to be “baseless” and its investigation “yielded zero evidence connecting Kerkhoff in any way to the construction, transportation, or planting of the pipe bombs.” Among the “extensive evidence of Kerkhoff’s innocence,” it says, is her alibi backed by evidence that she was at her home in Falls Church, Virginia, when the pipe bombs were placed on Jan. 5. The Blaze retracted its story on Dec. 4, the day of the news conference announcing the charges against Cole. The site wrote that while it stood by the sources, in light of the arrest, “we consider the values of fairness and accuracy to require retraction of this article.” In April, Kerkhoff sued Blaze Media alleging defamation, saying it “manufactured” the story to fit a “theory they had already decided to report.” The reporters, Kerkhoff’s attorneys wrote, “built their reporting careers on a single, unshakeable premise: that January 6, 2021 was a ‘deep state’ ‘inside job.’” Instead of investigating with an open mind, the attorneys wrote, the reporters “tried to confirm what they had already decided was true.” Her life “remains irrevocably altered: she was placed under FBI scrutiny that will follow her for the rest of her career, has lost friendships and professional opportunities, lives in fear for her physical safety, and has postponed her wedding — all because Blaze Media chose to manufacture a story rather than report the truth,” her attorneys wrote in court papers this week in the lawsuit, which is ongoing. The Blaze’s legal team has said that its stories didn’t directly identify Kerkhoff as the pipe bomber and that the story “went through multiple rounds of editorial review, including legal review and even review by Blaze Media executives.” Lawyers noted that Blaze Media terminated Baker and that his co-author resigned shortly thereafter, and that the publication is not responsible for any additional statements they’ve made. A message sent to The Blaze’s attorneys wasn’t immediately returned. Baker said in an interview with NBC News that he first noticed Kerkhoff when he was reviewing video from the Capitol attack. Baker had accused the government of riling up the crowd on Jan. 6, and he had been looking through publicly available video to find people carrying backpacks that might contain an “agitation weapon,” he said in an interview with NBC News. “It’s essentially a directed energy weapon that can either make you extremely agitated and behave in untoward ways, or it can debilitate you,” Baker said, referring to unusual crowd control tactics law enforcement has used in the past. He said he remains convinced that Cole is not the suspect. He believes the charges against Cole are part of a government cover-up, and that the government itself played some role with the pipe bombs. Kyle Seraphin, one of the special agents who performed surveillance in the case, has since left the FBI after a falling-out with Patel and now hosts a podcast. He said in an interview that he doesn’t believe the FBI’s accusations that Cole placed the bombs and that he expects a jury to acquit him. “There’s no way that a D.C. jury convicts this guy,” Seraphin said. Some of the attorneys representing Cole are also representing Baker and his co-author in the defamation lawsuit Kerkhoff filed. The government suggested during a hearing this month that it could pose a conflict. Meanwhile, Cole’s parents have given interviews saying the government is framing their son, including to former Fox News host Tucker Carlson — who downplayed Jan. 6 and fed a false narrative about the attack before his departure from the network — as well as Cara Castronuova, a former trainer on “The Biggest Loser” who is now a White House correspondent for a conservative outlet run by MyPillow founder Mike Lindell, a 2020 election denier. Enrique Tarrio, the head of the far-right Proud Boys, who was convicted of seditious conspiracy and serving a sentence of 22 years in federal prison until it was commuted by Trump, recently came out to support Cole, returning to the federal courthouse where he was tried. Tarrio said in an interview after the hearing that he considers Cole a part of the Jan. 6 community. “I think they should drop the case,” Tarrio said. “He’s a J6er.” Tarrio, who wore a “Brian Cole Did Nothing Wrong” T-shirt to the courthouse, said the Cole case undermines the judicial branch. “If you don’t have confidence in the system,” he said, “you get events like Jan. 6.”

articles.title: Schumer, Dems at odds as leader aims to kill Ohio Republican’s data center bill
articles.summary: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) is aiming to kill a bill sponsored by Republican Sen. Jon Husted (Ohio) to protect taxpayers from additional costs posed by AI-driven data centers, but his Democratic caucus isn’t fully on board after House Democrats overwhelmingly voted for the proposal. The looming Senate floor fight over artificial intelligence and…
articles.body:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) is aiming to kill a bill sponsored by Republican Sen. Jon Husted (Ohio) to protect taxpayers from additional costs posed by AI-driven data centers, but his Democratic caucus isn’t fully on board after House Democrats overwhelmingly voted for the proposal.

The looming Senate floor fight over artificial intelligence and data centers has big implications for the Ohio Senate race, where the Democratic challenger, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio), has made Husted’s support for data centers a central issue in the campaign.

Senate Democrats say something needs to be done to protect taxpayers from rising energy costs due to data center growth, but they see the Husted bill — the Ratepayer Protection Act, which attracted huge bipartisan support in the House — as a political life raft for the GOP incumbent, who is trailing in the polls.

“It seems like it’s kind of a political bailout,” said Democratic Sen. Tina Smith (Minn.), alluding to the political damage Husted has suffered after getting pummeled with ads framing him as “the face of data centers” who cut “sweetheart tax deals” for them.

A YouGov poll of 1,000 likely voters in Ohio conducted earlier this month found that 75 percent of respondents opposed or strongly opposed the construction of data centers in their local communities. Nearly half of Ohio voters — 47 percent — said a candidate’s stance on data centers is extremely important or very important to their vote in November.

Brown has spent more than $430,000 on online ads that talk about data centers, according to a study by Absecon Group, a public affairs group that studies media strategy.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is expected to file a cloture motion on Husted’s bill Monday, which would set up the first procedural vote to advance it on the floor Wednesday.

Republicans say there is heavy pressure on Democrats to vote for the bill after it passed the House by an overwhelming margin of 417-3 on Sept. 16. Only three House Democrats voted against it.

Schumer, however, is looking to quash Husted’s bill, which would deprive the vulnerable GOP incumbent of a political victory that he could use in the weeks ahead to defend himself from political attacks that he is Big Data’s ally in Washington.

But it will be a major test of his leadership strength whether he can convince almost his entire caucus to sink the bill.

Schumer on Wednesday dismissed Husted’s bill as a “fraud,” signaling that he will urge Democratic colleagues to block it on the floor later this week.

“Sen. Husted’s bill is a fraud, it’s voluntary, no company has to do it. The bill we have is mandatory. It is much stronger, and it is what is needed,” the New York senator said.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) — the ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, who blocked Husted’s bill on the floor last week when the Ohio Republican asked for unanimous consent to pass it — argued that it would not require data centers to pay the full cost of energy they consume.

“The Ratepayer Protection Act does nothing to meaningfully address the rising costs of AI data center development. Instead, it relies on a voluntary framework that does not require AI data centers to pay the full cost of the energy they consume or the strain they place on the grid,” he said.

Husted argues, however, that his bill would “force” data centers “to pay their own way” because it would outline a federal standard and require states to consider that standard when determining regulations for data centers.

“Many states have already said they want to protect ratepayers by making data centers pay for their own electricity grid and production—and his bill does just that,” said Olivia Tripodi, a spokesperson for Husted.

Some Democratic senators see Husted’s bill as a step in the right direction — albeit a modest step — and favor voting to proceed to his bill so that it can be debated and amended on the Senate floor.

“My view is that this is a tiny step forward, but we shouldn’t miss this opportunity to strengthen it,” said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen (Md.).

Van Hollen said Husted’s bill “doesn’t do nearly enough,” but he thinks Democrats will miss a valuable opportunity if they simply defeat the motion to proceed to the legislation.

“I’ve got a proposal called Power for the People Act that I’ve been trying to get passed for a while, which would actually protect ratepayers, make sure they don’t have to subsidize the richest corporations on the planet,” he said.

The Maryland Democrat said his colleagues should vote to get on Husted’s bill but not let it proceed to final passage unless Senate Republicans allow votes on amendments to strengthen it.

Van Hollen’s bill would direct states to consider whether to establish separate electricity rate classes for data centers so that they cover any higher energy costs they generate. And it would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to issue a rule to ensure data centers pay for transmission upgrades that would not otherwise be needed if they were not consuming massive amounts of energy.

Van Hollen said Democrats should “take the step of getting on the bill” while “making it clear” they will not advance it to final passage without substantial improvements.

But that’s a strategy that Schumer and other Senate leaders have avoided in recent years, calculating that once the Senate votes to begin debating legislation, it generates a lot of momentum and becomes much tougher to block the bill from moving to final passage.

Husted said that Democrats will find themselves on the political defensive if they block his bill this week, noting that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — both New York Democrats — along with “Democrats all on the House side voted for it and thought it was a great bill because they understood that it would lower energy prices.”

“And if Senate Democrats want to be the lone obstacle to passage, then shame on them,” Husted said. “That shows that they don’t really care about affordability.”

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), the ranking member on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, isn’t a fan of voting to begin debate on Husted’s bill — as some fellow Democratic senators are proposing.

“Everybody’s entitled to their views,” he said, arguing that a better approach would be to challenge Trump’s opposition to building out the nation’s clean-energy infrastructure to increase total energy supplies.

Whitehouse has negotiated the outlines of a permitting reform deal with Republicans that one Senate Democratic aide said would include Heinrich’s Guarding Ratepayers from Increased Demand-costs (GRID) Savings Act.

Senate Democrats say that the GRID Savings Act would actually require large-load customers like data centers to pay for the facilities they need to connect them to the energy grid.

But Whitehouse said the permitting deal needs to be put into legislative language, a lengthy process that he suggested couldn’t get done before senators are scheduled to adjourn for an extended preelection recess.

The muddled situation leaves some Democrats on the fence about how to vote on Husted’s bill next week.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), an outspoken critic of artificial intelligence who has called for a federal moratorium on building AI data centers, declined two requests to comment on Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act.

Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) said he hasn’t taken a position on Husted’s bill yet.

“I’d have to read it. I haven’t read it yet,” he said.

Other Democratic senators also told The Hill they remain undecided.

articles.title: Hispanic voters turn toward Democrats in redistricted Texas, Florida
articles.summary: Hispanic voters swung to the right in the last election, but Republicans appear to be losing ground with the key voting bloc, potentially complicating the party’s path to victory in the redistricted red strongholds of Texas, Florida and beyond. Recent polling has signaled that Hispanic voters who helped propel President Trump to a second term…
articles.body:
Hispanic voters swung to the right in the last election, but Republicans appear to be losing ground with the key voting bloc, potentially complicating the party’s path to victory in the redistricted red strongholds of Texas, Florida and beyond.

Recent polling has signaled that Hispanic voters who helped propel President Trump to a second term are shifting toward Democrats for the midterms, frustrated by the White House’s handling of the economy and controversial immigration policies.

Democrats are eager to recapture those voters as they fight to flip the House and Senate — particularly in Texas and Florida, the red states with the highest Hispanic populations in the country, and where Republicans redrew congressional maps to give themselves a midterm boost.

“In Texas and Florida, Republicans are losing ground with many of the Hispanic voters with whom they made major inroads in 2024. As a result, heavily Hispanic seats in South Texas and South Florida that voted for Trump by double digits are now hosting highly competitive races,” Cook Political Report analyst Erin Covey wrote on Friday as the election handicapper moved three Florida House races and three Texas House races toward Democrats.

Hispanic voters, who make up 16 percent of the national electorate, sided with former President Biden by 25 points in the 2020 presidential election, but former Vice President Kamala Harris won the group by just 3 points as the Democratic standard-bearer in 2024, according to Pew Research . In 2024, Trump carried the Latino bloc in Texas by about 10 points and in Florida by roughly 13 points .

Now, however, a Cook Political Report/Televisa Univision survey found that 18 percent of Hispanic voters who supported Trump in 2024 disapprove of the job he’s doing — and 22 percent do not support a Republican House candidate on a generic ballot.

Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) latest polling averages also show that Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico’s lead among Hispanic voters has jumped from 8 points this spring to a 23-point advantage over Republican Ken Paxton, with a similarly stark increase for Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the governor’s race.

This shift comes as the Latino electorate in Texas has more than doubled since 2000 , according to the Latino Policy and Politics Institute at the University of California, Los Angeles, to roughly 32 percent of the state’s eligible voters.

“There’s no question” the bloc has moved strongly toward Democrats in Texas since 2024, said Jon Taylor, a political science professor at the University of Texas at San Antonio. “I think this is why there was such an impetus on the part of Trump and Abbott to do this mid-decade redistricting.”

Lone Star State Republicans kick-started the national redistricting fight last year when they reshaped their House districts to give the party a five-seat boost, based on the 2024 results, including Hispanic Texans’ rightward shift.

But Republicans may ultimately gain nothing from the national back-and-forth over district lines, according to a DDHQ analysis last week, with Latino voters in Texas potentially playing a big role.

“As for why Texas Republicans aren’t adding as many seats as they hoped, potential Democratic holds (or gains) in red-leaning but heavily Latino districts in South Texas are the chief factor,” Geoffrey Skelley, DDHQ’s chief elections analyst, wrote.

“The biggest embarrassment for the Republicans will be these Texas races that they gerrymandered because they assumed that these Hispanic voters would perform the same way they had just a year ago for Donald Trump, and so that may end up being a dummymander,” said Chuck Rocha, a Hispanic Democratic strategist who’s served as a senior adviser to campaigns up and down the ballot, including Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vt.) presidential bids and Talarico’s Senate bid in Texas.

Similar shifts could be underway in Florida, where Republican-friendly redistricting has targeted as many as four Democratic-held seats. Latino voters make up roughly 29 percent of the Sunshine State’s population, according to census data.

In a late May poll from UnidosUS, 20 percent of Hispanic voters in Florida who backed Trump in 2024 said they would not repeat their vote. And a New York Times analysis this week found that, if the latest polls bear out, Florida could see multiple red seats swing sharply toward Democrats.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) put a spotlight on Latino voters’ importance in Florida last week when she asserted in a campaign advertisement that Trump had gone “too far” with federal immigration enforcement operations.

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” said Salazar in the ad for her reelection bid in the 27th Congressional District, which is projected to “lean Republican” by Cook Political Report. Trump said last week that he disagrees with Salazar, stressing that his tough stance on the southern border “probably at least partially won the election.” The congresswoman later said that Trump was “ very receptive ” to her warning.

House Republicans’ campaign arm has hailed this cycle’s GOP-friendly redistricting and continues to stress its cash advantage and airwave blitz as November nears, arguing that “House Dems are fighting to catch up with the limited resources they have.”

But Maria Cardona, a Democratic strategist who has long specialized in Hispanic outreach, argued that the GOP’s redistricting in Texas and Florida will “backfire” because “they were convinced that the gains that they made in ‘24 were permanent, and … anyone who thinks that has no clue about how Latino voters work.”

Alongside frustration over the White House’s immigration crackdown, economic concerns dominate. Pocketbook woes drove the blue-leaning bloc’s rightward shift in 2024 — and they now appear to be turning Hispanic voters back to Democrats.

“The exact same thing that is driving Hispanics away from Republicans is what drove them away from Democrats just two years ago,” said Mike Madrid, a Trump critic and Republican strategist who specializes in Latino voting behavior and trends.

“This is overwhelmingly about affordability, cost of living, and falling behind, and not being able to make it again as working-class people in this economy.”

The Cook Political Report survey showed that Hispanic voters in Texas rate economic concerns as more important to them in the election than immigration or Immigration and Customs Enforcement by a 2-to-1 margin.

Of course, turnout will be key to helping Democrats capitalize on Hispanic voters’ frustrations with the GOP. To that end, candidates such as Talarico in Texas are making notable investments in Spanish-language ads and other outreach efforts aimed at capturing disaffected Hispanic Texans.

But even if Hispanic voters do move toward Democrats in November, experts cautioned that the bloc could swing again if Democrats aren’t responsive to Hispanic voters’ concerns about the economy and other top issues.

“I think there’s a realignment. I think they’re frustrated with both parties, but right now, … Democrats are benefiting from the frustration,” Rocha said.

“I think that the Latino voter is going to become the new soccer mom, and everybody’s going to be trying to figure out how to get a swing voter in their camp, especially with 2028 on the horizon.”
