articles.title: Sports betting companies face image crisis this NFL season
articles.summary: The return of football season is bringing a major boom in sports gambling activity across the country, and with it, new scrutiny over how online sportsbooks are doing business. Major online betting providers like FanDuel and DraftKings are spending more than ever this fall on extensive advertising campaigns and corporate partnerships marketing themselves to potential…
articles.body:
The return of football season is bringing a major boom in sports gambling activity across the country, and with it, new scrutiny over how online sportsbooks are doing business.

Major online betting providers like FanDuel and DraftKings are spending more than ever this fall on extensive advertising campaigns and corporate partnerships marketing themselves to potential customers on national television and social media.

Across each of the major sports leagues, a growing number of teams, media companies and athletes are partnering directly with oddsmakers and sportsbooks and encouraging fans to put skin in the game.

It’s a phenomenon that’s become deeply embedded in the modern-day sports viewing experience, and it’s rubbing some fans the wrong way while alarming public health advocates.

“The concern here is not simply that sportsbook companies advertise; it is the perceived saturation of gambling throughout the sports-viewing experience,” said Matthew Bakowicz, a former operations official for DraftKings at Foxwoods Resort Casino.

“I think it is better described as a regulatory and cultural issue surrounding how gambling is marketed in the United States. The U.S. legalized sports betting very quickly across a large number of jurisdictions, and now policymakers are working through what the appropriate boundaries should be,” he added.

The entrance of unregulated prediction markets into the sports gambling space has drawn intense scrutiny from lawmakers on Capitol Hill and in statehouses in recent months.

Concerns about people in government or with access to sensitive insider information using prediction markets to profit off “event contracts” mirror concerns about corruption and game-rigging in pro sports, critics say.

It comes as lawmakers and public health advocates raise concern that more people are becoming addicted to online sports gambling and that the gaming industry is not doing enough to buck the trend.

“With these sportsbooks and sports leagues, one hasn’t corrupted the other, they’re in this together. So if their collective image is taking a hit, they’ve done it to themselves,” said Harry Levant, director of gambling policy at the Public Health Advocacy Institute. “What they’ve done is create a fundamentally different, inherently dangerous and effectively designed form of gambling that didn’t exist before.”

The multibillion-dollar sports gaming industry in the U.S. has spent the years since the Supreme Court lifted federal bans on sports betting reaping huge profits and using some of its revenues to lobby critics and government regulators.

It is estimated that sportsbooks and online casinos spent more than $200 million in digital and linear advertising in the first six months of 2026. Perhaps as a result of those efforts, there has been a 10 percent growth by prediction markets in the online sports betting space during the same period.

The competition has created lucrative endorsement opportunities for some of the biggest names in sports, with figures like Charles Barkley and Bryce Harper partnering directly in recent months with sportsbooks and casinos.

Some are finding there can be pitfalls to such partnerships.

Harper sparked controversy earlier this year when he recorded a personalized video for a FanDuel VIP who later sued the sportsbook for what he alleged was predatory behavior.

Officials within the sports gambling industry argue advertising budgets for sports betting companies are eclipsed by that of insurance companies like Geico or State Farm and food and beverage providers like Anheuser-Busch.

“Americans have always bet on sports. Legalization changed the policy, not the behavior,” said Joe Maloney, president of the Sports Betting Alliance. “The choice was never betting versus no betting. It is a regulated market with safeguards and oversight, or an illegal market with none.”

Most observers agree the speed with which sports gambling exploded in the U.S. after the 2018 Supreme Court ruling is the reason stricter guardrails on things like advertising and integrity monitoring have not caught up with the platforms.

Widespread fears about the emergence of new technologies are also not doing major gambling companies any favors in the public relations department.

A recent New York Times investigation found DraftKings, one of the nation’s largest online sportsbooks, is increasingly using artificial intelligence to offer special promotions and bonuses to gamblers who have a history of compulsive use or are deemed likely to lose.

Massachusetts is allegedly probing the company over the tactic.

In a statement to The Hill this week, a DraftKings spokesperson said the Times’s story is “built on false premises and is based on the limited accounts of a few former employees.”

“Promotions are designed to reward customers who engage with and remain loyal to DraftKings,” the spokesperson said. “We use data science and analytics (not AI) to customize promotions based on customer preferences, for example if a customer is interested in football and has never placed a bet on hockey, we do not send them hockey promotions—these are basic marketing practices.”

Studies have shown men aged 18-35 are most likely to use online sports gaming platforms, and some companies are getting increasingly aggressive in targeting that demographic.

Novig, a previously little-known sports prediction market platform earlier this month tapped actor Sydney Sweeney for an ad promoting the service that sparked controversy over the way it portrayed women in sports.

Sweeney appeared largely unclothed in the ad, which a number of female athletes argued was insulting and made a mockery of women in sports as part of a cynical marketing ploy.

“These companies are increasingly trying to compete in the attention economy with a moment of virality, and celebrities causing controversy can do that,” said Michael Tadesse, a professor of marketing at the George Washington University School of Business. “But that does not necessarily create fan loyalty, and that’s what we have to question.”

As more controversies relating to sports gambling culture in the U.S. pop up, some say major brands in sports could eventually show more hesitation before getting into bed with oddsmakers, others say.

“The reality is there is a lot of dollars coming in but there is a liability out there for an athlete or team’s brand taking a hit because of some negative story relating to gambling,” said Stephen Shapiro, chair of the University of South Carolina’s Department of Sport and Entertainment Management. “There’s some risk there. If they’re regularly partnering with these companies and the public perceives them more negatively over time, there could be some spillover.”

The Senate has officially teed up a final vote on the Protect College Sports Act, set for 5:30 p.m. EDT on Monday. It’s the culmination of a months-long effort by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) to pass legislation that would shield the NCAA from lawsuits around issues like eligibility, the transfer portal and revenue sharing. Senate Democrats failed to kill the bill over disagreements about unionization of student athletes and caps on coach and administrator salaries. Cruz has said he wants Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to call the House back into session before the midterm elections to take up the bill, but most observers say such a scenario is unlikely.

President Trump attended the University of Tennessee’s football game against the University of Texas in Knoxville, Tenn. The president has increasingly used sporting events and major sports moments as a bid to connect with voters. Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian surprised some when he revealed the logistical issues associated with having the president at a major college football game. “Any time he enters the stadium or leaves or changes locations, they cut all communications,” the Texas coach told reporters last week. “They cut headsets to coaches so … you have to have a plan for that, and you have no warning.”

The NFL fined San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk almost $15,000 last week for an endzone celebration in which he mimed drinking a beverage. The league said it thought the celebration was an “imitation of chugging a beer” and violated Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, according to ESPN. The outlet noted the NFL front office determined Juszczyk conducted himself in a way that did not reflect the NFL in a positive light and showed a lack of sportsmanship. Critics of the fine pointed out that Bud Light is the official beer sponsor of the NFL, and the two companies have done business together for years. Juszczyk, who is nicknamed “Juice,” defended himself by saying his celebration, which he has done for years, was him drinking juice, not beer.

Jocks on the Hill: Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.)

Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), an outgoing member of the House, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“I played a lot of cricket growing up. I still follow cricket, but now living in the U.S., I tend to be more about American football.”

“I follow all of the Detroit-based teams. Of course, I’m a big fan of the Lions.”

Is there an athlete you really admired growing up:

“The hockey guy … Steve Yzerman. I love him. He’s a legend, and I also loved all those Tigers players from back then like Kirk Gibson.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you really like to root against?

“I mean not really, I’m not a super hateful person. I like them all, I love what all the teams do.”

Why do you think sports brings people together in such politically divided times?

“Sports can help you and inspire you. Watching a close game and root for the underdog is great. You can sit on your couch and have all this energy without having to participate.”

The Athletic published an extensive interview with international soccer star Kylian Mbappé, during which he talked about “why he has just ended a near 20-year association with Nike, his chances of winning the Ballon d’Or next month and why he fully intends to keep speaking up for what he sees as good over bad.”

Sports Illustrated has a great profile of WNBA Hall-of-Famer Cheryl Reeve, the league’s winningest coach, a four-time league champion and a leader with a five-word mantra in life and basketball: “You get what you accept.”

Postseason baseball arrives this week, and this fall could be an exciting time in the Windy City, as the Chicago Tribune celebrates a “splendid moment” when both the White Sox and Cubs clinched playoff berths on Thursday for the first time since the COVID-shortened 2020 season, and before that since 2008.

articles.title: Woke megachurch pastor, Dem nominee called on congregation to repent for driving, eating beef
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton, the Democrat seeking to be the first Kansans sent to the Senate in nearly a century, once asked his church congregation to repent for eating beef.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: In Kansas, cows are king, but a Democrat trying to seize power once told his congregation to repent for eating beef and raising cattle. Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee running to unseat Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in the Sunflower State, for years led the largest United Methodist church in the nation. He would give sermons that Marshall charged were "woke," and counter to Kansans' values. One such sermon, reviewed by Fox News Digital, saw Hamilton call on his congregation to repent over their carbon footprints. GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS "That's what repentance means — I saw things differently, it changed my heart, and it changed my behavior," Hamilton said during a January 2020 sermon called, "What would Jesus say about climate change?" "So what I'm calling you to today, and I'm calling myself to it, because I've been wasteful, I've done things that wasn't, you know, I didn't think about it, how it wasn't really good stewardship of the earth around me," he continued. "I'm calling us to repentance to say, ‘I realize that this has impact, even if it seems small, it has an impact on the world and future generations. And I feel badly about that, and I'm going to do something different from this time forward.’" Despite Kansas’ 94-year history of being a ruby-red bastion for the GOP in the Senate, the race between Hamilton and Marshall has unexpectedly tightened in recent months as Republicans across the country face a sobering political environment. BIG MONEY PROPELS DEM MEGACHURCH PASTOR TO VICTORY IN LONGSHOT KANSAS SENATE BID Kansas slipped from "Likely R" in Fox News’ Power Rankings to "Lean R," and Cook Political Report echoed the same shift, too. "In a state with more cattle than people, Hamilton saying that Kansans need repent for eating too much beef and flip flopping on the Farm Bill proves he’d be just like every other liberal Democrat in the Senate," Marshall told Fox News Digital in a statement. High fuel prices, particularly diesel in an agriculture-centric state like Kansas, spurred by President Donald Trump’s Iran war are giving voters anxiety, and expanding the map of battleground states that Republicans need to defend to maintain their majority in the Senate. Hamilton's campaign countered to Fox News Digital that Marshall has "repeatedly introduced legislation to reduce emissions from cattle and claimed 'everyone's concerned about the methane production in the cattle industry.'" "Marshall even bragged how the decline of the herd 'eliminated half of the methane gas produced from cattle already,'" Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton, said. "As Adam said at the debate, Roger should repent for failing to stand up for Kansas cattle producers on tariffs, foreign imports, and skyrocketing diesel prices, and now he should repent for attacking Adam for something Roger Marshall said himself in the Senate. Kansas producers don't need lectures from someone who voted to put warning labels on hot dogs and bacon." Meanwhile, Hamilton’s sermon was part scripture, part PowerPoint presentation on how greenhouse gases occur and their impact on the environment. And during his 44-minute talk, Hamilton suggested that one of Kansas’ staple economic drivers, beef, was a major contributor to the problem. 'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN "Some of the things that we grow, because we like to eat them, like cattle, end up producing more carbon dioxide than other crops that we could grow, other forms of food that we could have," Hamilton said. "And so, in all of these ways, we are creating or adding to the amount of greenhouse gases in our world." Cattle is a major industry for Kansas, which is the nation’s third-largest producer of beef, according to the Kansas Livestock Association. There are more heads of cattle in the state, just over 5.8 million, than people, with the state’s population sitting at roughly 2.9 million. It provides a major cash influx for the state’s economy, too, with cattle farming and ranching producing tens of billions of dollars and employing over tens of thousands of Kansans. "It is disappointing that a candidate for the U.S. Senate in Kansas, one of the nation’s top beef-producing states, would make a statement like this to his parishioners about beef’s impact on the climate," Kansas Livestock Association Chief Executive Officer Matt Teagarden told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Beef is an important, nutritious part of the American diet, and cattle play a significant role in maintaining grassland health and conservation, while accounting for only 2% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Still, six years ago, Hamilton was calling on his congregation to change their habits to reduce their carbon footprint. "Now, you got to do everything you can to reduce your own usage of fossil fuels, but maybe changing your diet so that the things that you eat are requiring less production that creates methane and carbon dioxide and everything else," Hamilton said.

articles.title: Trump posts series of attacks on GOP congresswoman who criticized him on immigration
articles.summary: President Donald Trump appeared to intensify his irritation with GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar on Saturday evening after reposting a series of social media a...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump reposted a series of critical social media comments about GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar on Saturday evening after the congresswoman made waves last week for breaking with him on his immigration tactics.

The president shared in quick succession on Truth Social at least 14 posts from other users critical of Salazar, who is facing a tough reelection race in Florida as Republicans' midterm fortunes decline.

"She is nothing but a back stabber. I'm glad the Latino support hasn't wavered," one user wrote in a post shared by Trump.

Another user slammed the congresswoman: "She wants amnesty for the ppl how criminally crossed our borders defying our laws."

"So we need a NEW Republican to Replace Salazar," a different user said .

When asked about the social media posts, a White House official told CNN, "It's unfortunate she has her view, but that is not the President's. The President campaigned on a strong border, which was a large reason as to why he won by a landslide in 2024."

CNN also reached out to Salazar's office and reelection campaign for comment on the reposts.

Salazar, who represents a heavily Hispanic district, drew Trump's ire last week after she broke with the president in a new ad ahead of the midterms. The congresswoman addresses Trump directly in the ad, speaking straight to the camera as she says, "some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far."

Salazar points to statistics she said show that 50% of the people detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in July "had no criminal record."

Following the ad's release, Trump confirmed in response to a question from a reporter that he had seen the ad and still backed the Florida congresswoman, even though he did not share her view.

"I disagree with her," Trump said in the Oval Office. He claimed that Salazar "got a little bit soft on the border" and wouldn't have won without his endorsement.

Salazar told "Face The Nation" that she had a "very good conversation" with the president after releasing the campaign ad and characterized Trump as "very receptive" to her warning that Hispanic voters feel "betrayed" ahead of the midterm election.

The congresswoman's ad comes as ICE increased immigration arrests nationwide over the summer. In August, for example, ICE took around 51,000 people into custody, setting a new high under the second Trump administration. The previous high had been set the month prior when the agency took more than 46,000 people into custody in July.

This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: White House reporters float some surprise choices on which Republicans could run for president after Trump
articles.summary: White House reporters were asked who among Republicans may enter the 2028 presidential race during a panel discussion at the Texas Tribune Festival.
articles.body: AUSTIN, Texas — Three prominent White House reporters discussed which Republicans could run to succeed President Donald Trump in 2028 — and floated a wide range of names. Politico White House bureau chief Dasha Burns, NBC News chief White House correspondent Garrett Haake and New York Times White House correspondent Maggie Haberman sat down for a panel discussion about covering the Trump presidency Friday at the Texas Tribune Festival. While much of the discussion focused on Trump's current term in office, moderator Annah Aschbrenner of The Washington Post finished the conversation by asking how the "competition" will shape up in the next election. RAHM EMANUEL TOUTS WHAT SEPARATES HIM FROM OTHER DEMS AS HE MULLS 2028 PRESIDENTIAL BID "I think there are four lanes to the Republican Party," Haake responded. "I think one lane is the Trump successor, the sort of like, from the inside of the White House, who's the person who gets blessed... Presumably, that's JD Vance. Unless JD Vance decides, for whatever reason, [he] doesn't want it, or is somehow disqualified, then maybe it's Marco Rubio." "Then I think there's the 'I tried to help you, but you didn't listen' lane, which is like Ted Cruz, somebody who's going to spend the next two years making Trump's closest ally, fight real hard, but then when it comes around saying, you know, it didn't work, [Trump's] approval rate is 25%, here's what I told him to do, he didn't listen," he continued. "Then I'd think there is this explicitly anti-Trump lane, which is somebody like if Chris Christie... maybe it's [outgoing Nebraska Congressman] Don Bacon or somebody like that." Haake then shared what he called his "fourth wild card," which was HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., sparking gasps and groans from the largely liberal audience. Burns jumped in, adding former DNI Tulsi Gabbard to Haake's fourth lane of candidates. TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028 Haake theorized that if the MAGA coalition is fractured by 2028, the "MAHA group" — the Make America Healthy Again movement that helped fuel RFK Jr.'s independent run for president in 2024 and ultimately rallied behind Trump could rally behind the ex-Democrat, who he said "owns" that constituency more than Trump. Haberman seemed to agree with Haake's assessment, adding the "asterisk" that it's "likely JD Vance's nomination if he wants it" but that the war with Iran could also impact his chances. While she stopped short of adding his name to the list of GOP hopefuls, Burns stressed the major influence Donald Trump Jr. has within the Republican Party, telling the crowd that Vance would not have been vice president without him. CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS "He is still enormously popular among the MAGA crowd," Burns said. "He has a very different relationship, actually, than his dad does." "He speaks the language of conservatives more," Haberman chimed in. The Politico Playbook co-author then recalled Trump Jr. introducing his father at campaign rallies and how he'd receive "massive ovations" to the point that Trump would come out and remark on the enthusiasm for his son. Burns said Trump Jr. eventually stopped introducing his father as a result. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So there's a world where Don Jr. really brings a ton of the coalition to JD Vance, and that will, I think, largely be positive for him," Burns said. "I think that what is happening with these midterms, if it is the bloodbath that all the numbers are saying will be . . . I think the floodgates open, and it really changes the 2028 dynamics." Burns added that a "ton of people" from Trump's cabinet could throw their hat in the ring in addition to RFK Jr. and Gabbard, also citing Secretary of War Pete Hegseth as a potential contender.

articles.title: Data center developers should have known how much Americans love their land
articles.summary: The data center backlash is intensifying. In fact, more Americans now oppose data centers than fear AI. This is true even though tech companies have plausible defenses to much of the backlash. Data centers, for example, use far less water than the nation’s golf courses. There is little evidence so far that they significantly raise…
articles.body:
The data center backlash is intensifying. In fact, more Americans now oppose data centers than fear AI.

This is true even though tech companies have plausible defenses to much of the backlash. Data centers, for example, use far less water than the nation’s golf courses. There is little evidence so far that they significantly raise energy rates . Data centers can generate huge tax revenues that help finance police and school budgets. Also, do you really want China to lead the race for a technology that will revolutionize just about everything, including armed conflict?

What the tech companies cannot defend is the scale of these monstrosities and their location in places near where people live. According to the Pew Research Center, 42 percent of Americans live within 5 miles of “an existing or planned data center.” The tech companies’ siting decisions may serve their operational convenience , but they threaten the bond between Americans and their land and homes.

Take Ida Huddleston and her daughter, Delsia Bare, in Mason County, Kentucky. They made headlines by turning down a $33 million offer from a data center developer for their 650-acre farm. “My whole entire life is nothing but the land,” Ida explained to reporters. Delsia added, “There’s a bond with the land. That’s family, that’s history.”

That bond runs deep in our history. The prospect of owning land drew early settlers to America from Europe, because hacking their own farms out of the wilderness was better than living by someone else’s leave. George Washington is supposed to have said, “I had rather be on my farm than be emperor of the world.”

Near the end of the Civil War, Union General William Tecumseh Sherman met with Black ministers in Savannah, Georgia, and asked them what the newly freed slaves needed most. “The way we can best take care of ourselves is to have land,” they replied. Land meant a livelihood, political independence , and self-respect.

Industrialization forced people off their land, but there were fights. In the 1930s, the New Deal’s Tennessee Valley Authority dammed rivers in Tennessee for flood control and to build hydroelectric plants. Thousands of families had to abandon their homes; entire graveyards were dug up and relocated. But Mattie Randolph in Campbell County, brandishing a shotgun, refused to leave the farm she had bought after years as a sharecropper. TVA workers tied a rowboat to Mattie’s porch and, with the water rising, she and her family finally left to save themselves. The TVA thought Mattie was a backward hick, but she just didn’t want to give up her land.

To many, losing a view to a data center is akin to having their land taken away. Much of the data center backlash comes from organizations such as Our Land , Our Home, Our Harford, which was organized in Harford County, Maryland to fight data centers. “I couldn’t stand the thought of my kids, my grandkids never wanting to visit me because there would be an industrial site right across the street,” explained organizer Krissy Flatau.

In Leon County, Texas, a proposed data center that would destroy 1,200 acres of woods and farmland provoked a fierce grassroots backlash . “Why take green fields for this?” asked fifth-generation rancher Rachel Streater.

In her 2016 song, “ Farewell to Green Valleys,” Emmy Award-winning musician Connie Dover expressed the grief inflicted by powerful developers on the helpless people of Platte County, Missouri. “Farewell to green valleys and wide open skies, goodbye to the sunset and the clear twilight hour. What shall we behold when our beauty is gone? Have you heard the news boys, Platte County’s for sale.”

Unless tech companies change where they build these data centers and their scale, sad laments like that are not going away — and neither is the backlash.

Gregory J. Wallance , a writer and former federal prosecutor in the Carter and Reagan administrations , is the author of, most recently, “Into Siberia: George Kennan’s Epic Journey Through the Brutal, Frozen Heart of Russia . ” Becket Adams has the week off.

articles.body:
President Trump fumed online over the weekend as Republicans face warning signs in Florida, going after a key ally who broke with him on immigration and brushing off the idea that another is trying to keep him at arm’s length.

Once a key battleground, the Sunshine State has increasingly shifted red since Trump’s first term. With an expected favorable midterm environment, Democrats are hoping they may be able to pick off a few House seats and even have a shot at winning statewide for the first time in years.

One of those potentially vulnerable House Republicans is Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (Fla.), who released an ad earlier this month accusing Trump of “going too far” in his immigration crackdown. She said the Hispanic voters who helped him get elected in 2024 “feel betrayed today.”

Salazar said last week that the president was “very receptive” to her warning about Hispanic voters and was a “gentleman” about it. But he seemingly changed his tune Saturday, reposting several other Truth Social users who criticized Salazar and suggested Trump shouldn’t support her anymore.

“She is nothing but a back stabber,” a post from one user read .

“Primary her in two years and see how she likes to keep criticising Trump then,” another reposted comment read .

Trump also reposted a Washington Post story detailing how Salazar is receiving backlash from some of her constituents who are frustrated with her for breaking with the president.

While few Republicans have been so strident in their breaks with Trump, Salazar is among a growing group within the president’s party seeking more distance from the White House in anticipation of a rough midterm election in November.

Salazar’s fellow Florida House Republican, Rep. Byron Donalds , who is running for governor, raised eyebrows after a few references to Trump were removed from his website .

The old layout of the website highlighted Trump’s endorsement of Donalds in a top banner, while the new one only shows his endorsement along with the ones that Donalds received from Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and others.

A Donalds campaign spokesperson said the congressman is still proud to have the president’s support and is focusing on the issues that matter most to Floridians. Donalds called Trump’s agenda “common sense” shortly after the website change when questioned about it.

Trump, in another post over the weekend , accused media outlets of reporting “Another Fake Story.”

“If Florida thought the story that Byron ‘dropped’ me was true, he would lose the Election, and that would be a terrible thing because he’s going to be a fantastic Governor!” he wrote on Truth Social.

Donalds and Salazar are trying to fend off Democratic opponents who are seeking to pull off what seemed to be longshot victories.

Salazar represents a district that has been solidly Republican for years, but two elections forecasters have shifted her district’s rating from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican” in the past week.

Democrats are now eyeing a handful of potential flip opportunities in Florida, despite Republicans redrawing the state’s congressional map earlier this year to favor themselves.

Some mixed polling has also suggested the Florida gubernatorial race, in which Donalds is facing former Rep. David Jolly , a Republican-turned-Democrat, could be more competitive than originally expected.

Decision Desk HQ even shifted its rating of the race to “Toss Up” last week as some polls showed a close contest. The race has since gone back to “lean Republican.”

A recent poll showed the Senate race tied. Though a possible outlier, it stoked optimism that Democrat Angie Nixon has a shot of upsetting Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.).

Flipping a statewide race in Florida may be too much for Democrats even in a good year, but a close race at the top of the ballot may help candidates further down, even in a district like Salazar’s.

In both races, the Hispanic vote may prove pivotal. Trump made notable gains with this demographic in 2024 as part of his strong victory in the state.

But as The Hill’s Julia Mueller reports for Insider, the GOP now seems to be losing ground with the key voting bloc. Sign up for Insider and read more here as Mueller explores a potentially seismic shift that complicates the party’s path in Florida, Texas and elsewhere.

Trump and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had dinner together Sunday evening at the White House in the aftermath of Amodei’s warnings about the risks posed by AI development. Trump has mostly dismissed concerns from lawmakers and industry leaders, who are pushing for more regulation.

The White House aired another taxpayer-funded ad ahead of the midterms during two NFL games Sunday, featuring Trump saying, “this is the final battle,” CNN reported . This is at least the third such ad to be released recently, leading to scrutiny from Democrats, some Republicans and a government watchdog group.

SpaceX is planning to launch the world’s most powerful rocket, known as Starship, into orbit this morning for the first time. The company plans for the rocket to make about six orbits over a nearly 10-hour period. The launch window will open at 8:15 a.m. EDT, provided no setbacks.

Sam Houston quarterback Landyn Locke (8) drops back for a pass during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Texas Tech on Sept. 26, 2026, in Lubbock, Texas. (AP Photo/Chase Seabolt)

BUSINESS TIME : The Senate is expected to hold a final vote today on key bipartisan legislation creating federal oversight for college athletics as one of its last major acts before its recess ahead of the midterms.

The upper chamber will depart Washington at the end of the week for a monthlong recess. The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi reports for Insider that Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is hoping to make the most of its remaining days.

The Protect College Sports Act, which was introduced by Cruz and Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), would implement several measures concerning the NCAA and its schools and athletes. It would protect the NCAA from antitrust lawsuits, set caps on revenue sharing and allow schools to have retention funds for their star players.

The bill would also require agents to register with a state before representing student-athletes and cap their fees at 5 percent and guarantee scholarships for 10 years after eligibility, allowing athletes to complete their degrees after their playing days are over.

The legislation has received pushback from some groups, including the Congressional Black Caucus, NAACP and AFL-CIO. But the Senate comfortably moved to advance the bill earlier this month in a 74-24 vote, making it likely to pass again on the final vote Monday.

“Not everyone got everything they wanted. Frankly, I didn’t. And neither did my counterpart, ranking member Maria Cantwell. But this is what legislating means,” Cruz said in remarks defending the bill last week.

Presuming the bill does pass, it would still need to get through the House before reaching the president’s desk.

AIR BASE ARREST : Five men were arrested Sunday on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack on an air base in the United Kingdom used by the U.S. for some actions against Iran.

London Metropolitan Police said officers received a call at 12:45 a.m. local time related to three suspicious vehicles that seemed to be traveling toward RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base operated by the U.S. under a longstanding agreement. The base has been used by U.S. bombers for limited strikes against Iranian missile sites.

Officials are investigating a link between the arrests and Iran as a possibility. Iran previously indicated that it considered the base to be a legitimate target.

Trump praised law enforcement for making the arrests, calling it “fantastic.” He said the federal government had been investigating the men.

Police feared an explosion was coming and arrested the men on suspicion of violating the U.K.’s Explosives Act. Aerial footage from Sky News seemed to show a bomb disposal robot traveling between the three vehicles.

THE HILL EXCLUSIVE : A pair of House Republicans are calling on the Trump administration to resume sanctions on a Russian-owned refinery in Serbia.

The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports GOP Reps. Joe Wilson (S.C.) and Keith Self (Texas) sent a letter to the Treasury Department on Friday pushing against extended sanctions relief for Serbia’s Russian-owned energy company, NIS.

The U.S. has repeatedly issues sanctions waivers for NIS since the company was blacklisted in January 2025. NIS supplies 80 percent of Serbia’s energy needs but is majority owned by the U.S.-sanctioned energy giants Gazprom Neft and Gazprom.

NIS applied for another waiver last week ahead of a Sept. 30 deadline.

“Furthermore, Serbia continues to maintain close political and economic ties with Russia and, unlike most European countries, has not imposed sanctions on Moscow following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022,” Wilson and Self said.

The House will convene at noon for a pro forma session.

Work continues on the White House ballroom on Sept. 25, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

THE MAGIC WORDS : The Trump administration has increasingly leaned on “national security” as a buzzword when providing its rationale for a wide range of controversial actions.

That was most recently on display last week following Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The president first made clear that his reasoning was because of frustration with their reporting, but he soon shifted to an argument about national security.

“Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World,” he said in a Truth Social post.

Trump has also made that argument for why the White House needs a ballroom, why he needs to build a massive arch, why he must be allowed to issue a sweeping tariff plan and why National Guardsmen must be deployed domestically.

But The Hill’s Sophie Brams reports that argument may be wearing thin in the courts.

“When the administration makes outlandish claims on the whole range of public policy matters, it’s natural that courts would scrutinize its national security claims more carefully,” said Matthew Waxman , a law professor at Columbia University and former national security official during the George W. Bush administration.

The administration has seen some success in making this argument. Waxman noted that the Supreme Court tends to avoid “second-guessing” the executive branch on national security issues, giving it wide deference.

But when the argument is stretched, the administration could run into trouble, Brams reports.

Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, speaks before President Trump arrives at the United States Army War College in Carlisle, Pa., during the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit on July 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Matt Rourke)

‘EVERYTHING UP FRONT’ : Mike Waltz , the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations,said the president rejected Iran’s ceasefire proposal over the weekend because Tehran asked for “everything up front.”

Waltz told CNN’s Jake Tapper during his “State of the Union” appearance Sunday that Iran wanted immediate relief from billions of dollars in sanctions. He said they also wanted snapback sanctions from the United Nations that have been in place for years to be lifted.

Trump confirmed Saturday that he turned down a ceasefire proposal, saying it “wouldn’t be acceptable.” The proposal would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz and resumed nuclear talks in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, The Wall Street Journal reported .

The deal would have instituted a seven-day ceasefire during an initial trust-building phase.

“They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters.

Waltz said Iranian officials are “miscalculating” that Trump is taking politics into consideration.

He said on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” that Iran’s proposal was a “cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable.”

The Journal reported that Trump has told aides that a renewed bombing campaign against Iran will likely happen after the midterms.

United in debt: America has become a nation of fake rich people , John Mac Ghlionn writes in The Hill.

The future is here: What will a Millennial-Gen Z majority mean for America? Adam Brandon writes in The Hill.

Tourists take photos in Grand Teton National Park, Wyo., on Aug. 14, 2022. (AP Photo/Jae C. Hong)

And finally … Major League Baseball has reportedly approached the Trump administration about hosting a baseball game at Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming.

The Washington Post reported that the administration has scouted locations inside the park located in the Rocky Mountains. An MLB official told the Post that the league approached the administration following the success of other stand-alone events, such as the Field of Dreams game in Iowa.

The White House told the outlet that MLB asked if hosting a game at a national park was possible and is not being directed by the administration, nor is it a priority. Still, if it were to happen, constructing a sports facility at Grand Teton could set a new precedent for the use of vast national park land, the Post reported.

articles.title: AOC's Ivy League warmup act leads democratic socialists in notorious anti-Israel chant
articles.summary: Cornell University's Young Democratic Socialists of America lead "from the river to the sea" chant before Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez takes stage.
articles.body: An event for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., saw her far-left hosts at Cornell University lead a packed crowd in singing the anti-Israel slogan "from the river to the sea" on Sunday. The Cornell University Young Democratic Socialists of America hosted the event for AOC, which her campaign labeled as a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall. The group's president, Mina Petrova, and co-Chair Zoe Reisman led the crowd of roughly 2,000 people in chanting "from the river to the sea," after declaring, "long live the student intifada." "Cornell is fundamentally a capitalist institution that prioritizes billionaires and profit over students and community and is controlled by CEO trustees that are profiting off of genocide and war," Petrova told the crowd at one point, triggering applause. BACKLASH ERUPTS OVER HASAN PIKER’S UPCOMING SPEAKING ENGAGEMENT AT CORNELL "Here we stand as anti-imperialists and believe that nobody is disposable. We have a responsibility to stand in solidarity with oppressed peoples everywhere," Reisman said. "Student activism is not dead. Long live student resistance, and long live the student intifada." YDSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital. 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS AOC made no apologies when she eventually took the stage, joining her young hosts in accusing Cornell of censorship. "Whether it’s the issue about Palestine or many others, whether it’s about people trying to fire those who are forming a union in their workplace, whether it’s people trying to speak up about a number of different issues, we have to respond to that first crackdown," she said. AOC’S SOCIALIST CREDENTIALS FACE FRESH SCRUTINY AFTER GLARING 7-YEAR GAP SURFACES: ‘VERY CONVENIENT’ "When we come out in numbers, they cannot take us all," she added. AOC's campaign says it is aimed at boosting voter turnout in Democrat strongholds, but recent polling shows that most Americans dislike association with Democratic Socialists of America groups. HOUSE REPUBLICAN AIMS TO PUT DEMOCRATS ON THE RECORD OVER DSA WITH RESOLUTION CONDEMNING SOCIALISM According to a recent Fox News Poll, 55% of registered voters hold an unfavorable view of the DSA, while only three in 10 see the DSA in a positive light. The Fox News Poll is the latest national survey to show that while the DSA has gained traction among Democrats, the group and the broader socialist movement in America face significant national skepticism. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The figures appear to reinforce a key element in the GOP midterm playbook, which aims to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election. Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump's Taxpayer-Funded Ads Draw Bipartisan Criticism
articles.summary: Critics have called the ads “propaganda,” but the White House says they’re “public service announcements.”
articles.body:
President Donald Trump declares that "this is the final battle" in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November's midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.

The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against "the deep state," "warmongers," "globalists," "Marxists," "communists," and "fascists."

Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023 , but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump's campaign and fine print saying it was "Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc." This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: "Paid for by the U.S. Government."

CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday , citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.

A second advert with the same "paid for by the U.S. government" disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song "Love Me" by singer-songwriter JMSN , showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like "largest tax cuts in history" and "reigniting American manufacturing." This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he "would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign."

A third , which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump's speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.

The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.

Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said : "I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves." (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem , who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)

When asked about the "Love Me" ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán . "It's inappropriate," Tillis told reporters .

Rep. Thomas Massie , a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the "Final Battle" ad: "Don't worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics."

Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the "Love Me" ad's production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad "does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions." Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: "How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?"

In another Sept. 24 letter , congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the "Love Me" ad should be taken off the air, as it was "the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars."

But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, " public service announcements ." A White House official told TIME Friday that the ads weren't political, didn't have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.

A spokesperson instead said that the ads were "about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad."

Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for "publicity or propaganda."

The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is "purely partisan," "self-aggrandizing," or "covert." But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.

Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act , the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren't. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.

In defense of the "public service announcements," the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure .)

"When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called 'public education,'" the Trump White House said. "When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it 'propaganda.'"

articles.title: Democrats have already proven we can deliver on affordability
articles.summary: Outgoing Rep. Steny Hoyer argues that Democrats proved effective governance during the 117th Congress through landmark legislation like the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act, urging voters to choose leaders capable of addressing the ongoing affordability crisis.
articles.body:
It’s hard to ignore the biggest challenge facing working families. Prices are ticking up at the grocery checkout at every visit. Gas costs well over $4 a gallon — even higher in some places. It was more expensive to run the air conditioner this summer. Medical bills are rising, and housing costs continue to increase while inflation is moving faster than growth in wages. It’s no surprise that both parties have been trying to make the 2026 election about affordability.

Republicans, however, can’t deliver. They’re fixated on a war of choice that’s spiking the price of oil, on spending billions to unleash poorly trained ICE agents on our communities, and on giving President Trump and those closest to him sweetheart deals and immunity from prosecution. They’re even doing everything they can to make the affordability crisis worse. They’ve taken the largest axe to Medicaid in history, supported tariffs that cost families thousands of dollars more a year, and made insurance costlier by refusing to extend tax credits under the Affordable Care Act .

More and more, the common refrain is that Washington simply isn’t showing up for working families — because it never does. That cynicism is exactly what Republicans bank on. Convince people to throw their hands up and believe neither party can or will do anything for them — all while riling up their base with sensationalized arguments about social and cultural divisions.

That refrain is wrong. I know that Congress can deliver on the economy because that’s what Democrats proved four years ago. In August 2022, when I was House majority leader, Congress sent President Joe Biden the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act to sign.

The first invested tens of billions of dollars in rebuilding American manufacturing and strengthening supply chains in order to bring consumer prices down. The second targeted energy prices, lowered healthcare costs, made it cheaper and easier to file taxes, and required the largest companies finally to pay their fair share. In one month, our Democratic majority delivered more on affordability, innovation and accountability than the Republican majority has in nearly four years since.

We had tight voting margins and profound disagreements — but we still governed effectively. The 117th Congress, which was held from 2021-2023, remains one of the most productive in modern history. The two affordability and economic-development laws we enacted in August 2022 were only part of that story.

In November 2021, Democrats achieved what Republicans had promised for years but never delivered: a bipartisan infrastructure law that put more than half a trillion dollars toward creating jobs, upgrading water and energy systems to keep consumer costs down, and making high-speed internet less expensive for rural and underserved communities. When we held power, Democrats implemented our Make It In America plan that invested in creating jobs, lowering costs for families, and building the infrastructure a modern economy needs to compete and grow.

For Americans who are struggling with high prices, it can be easy to tune Washington out, to write Congress off as a broken institution. But that’s exactly why people need to engage and participate. Judge those in power by what they do with it when they have it. Reward those who meet the moment — and reject those who can’t.

I’m retiring at the end of the year after more than four decades in Congress. I’ve seen progress and paralysis. I’ve experienced the warmest collegiality and the coldest confrontation. When I think back to what we achieved in the 117th Congress — on what Democrats were able to deliver for the people on affordability and economic progress when we held power — I’m reminded that closely divided government does not have to mean ineffective governing. When leaders are willing to seek consensus, make tough choices, and stay focused on improving people’s lives, Washington can and does deliver.

So, let’s make sure the next Congress is led by those ready to roll up their sleeves, work together despite party labels, and meet the high expectations Americans ought to have for those in power. Frankly, we can’t afford not to.

Steny H. Hoyer represents Maryland’s 5th District and served as House majority leader in the 110th, 111th, 116th and 117th congresses.

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s classic ‘9 to 5’ returning to theaters for limited run
articles.summary: The newly restored film will screen Oct. 9 through Oct. 15.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The classic 1980 workplace comedy “ 9 to 5 ” is returning to theaters next month for a special weeklong run.

The newly restored version of the film, starring the late Dolly Patrton, Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, will be shown in theaters nationwide from Oct. 9-15.

Directed by Colin Higgins, “9 to 5” follows three women office workers who join forces to get revenge on their sexist and demanding boss.

The film became a hit following its release and is remembered for its comedic take on workplace sexism, as well as Parton’s iconic title song , “9 to 5,” according to the Hollywood Reporter .

The theatrical re-release gives audiences a chance to see the beloved comedy on the big screen more than four decades after its original release.

Disney will donate net proceeds from each U.S. ticket purchase to The Dollywood Foundation,” Deadline reported . Proceeds will be used to support the country icon’s Imagination Library .

Parton died of cancer last month at age 80. She built an impressive legacy over the decades as a singer-songwriter, actor, philanthropist and entrepreneur — leaving big and small ways to honor the musician.

articles.title: Iran says it's up to Trump to choose between war and diplomacy
articles.summary: As the war with Iran hits the 7-month mark, Trump tells Axios he expects talks to resume despite neither side signaling willingness to change demands.
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran is "fully prepared for the war to be resumed," and also for the possibility of renewed diplomacy with the U.S. aimed at ending the seven-month conflict, and it's "up to President Trump to choose."Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday that he expected talks with Iran to resume this week , insisting again that the Islamic Republic is "losing badly" and eager to strike a peace deal. Last week, Iran proposed a seven-day ceasefire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, contingent upon the U.S. meeting conditions laid out in the mid-June memorandum of understanding , which fell apart after several weeks. Mr. Trump publicly rejected the new Iranian proposal last week, and Iran has insisted it will not change its demands.

U.S. and Iran expected to continue talking this week through mediators, official tells Reuters

The U.S. and Iran are expected to have separate talks with mediators on Monday or Tuesday, an official with knowledge of the negotiations told the Reuters news agency.

With Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in the U.S., as well as Qatari mediators, the talks are set to focus on an updated version of the 7-day proposal Iran gave to U.S. counterparts last week during the United Nations General Assembly, the official told Reuters.

President Trump said Sunday that he expected talks with Iran to resume in the coming days , a day after he rejected a new proposal put forward by Tehran last week for a seven-day ceasefire and phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios . "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."

Saudi Arabia's strategic East-West Crude Oil Pipeline operational again, Bloomberg says

Saudi Arabia has resumed exporting oil using its crucial East-West Crude Oil Pipeline after drone strikes earlier this month forced it shut, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter quoted by Bloomberg .

Saudi Arabia had been using the pipeline to transport oil from its eastern production hubs to its Red Sea ports for export - a vital alternative route as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has remained severely disrupted by the U.S.-Iran war.

The pipeline was shut down earlier this month after a series of drone attacks that Saudi authorities blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

The state-run energy giant Saudi Aramco, which operates the kingdom's oil infrastructure, tested the pipeline last week and has now resumed overseas shipments via the Red Sea route, a source familiar with the operation told Bloomberg.

Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have vowed to impose a blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports and against Saudi ships, and they have targeted several vessels in the region.

Iran lodges complaint with U.N. over U.S. sanctions on its aviation industry

Iran has lodged a complaint with the United Nations over U.S. sanctions against its aviation sector, which have forced the cancellation of many flights across the region, state media reported Monday.

The U.S. imposed restrictions this month on the entire Iranian aviation industry and vowed to take a hard line against any companies or countries that continue to assist it.

As the sanctions took effect last Wednesday, some major airlines were forced to cancel international flights as several nations in the region implemented bans.

"To defend the legitimate rights of the aviation industry and counter illegal restrictions imposed by America, Iran has drafted and submitted a formal protest to the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)," said civil aviation chief Abouzar Shiroudi, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.

Ayatollah Khamenei says U.S. forces will soon be pushed back

Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has been quoted as predicting that U.S. military forces will soon be driven out of the Arabian Sea.

In a message to mark Iran's Sacred Defense Week, the ayatollah - who has not been seen or heard from directly since the war began - said U.S. forces were unable to advance beyond the Arabian Sea, which leads to the Strait of Hormuz, "because of the painful blows they have received."

He added that soon, U.S. troops would be driven from the Arabian Sea, too.

U.S. forces have operated across the region since the war began, including to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in defiance of Iran's bid to control traffic through the vital waterway.

The wide-ranging message attributed by Iranian state media to Khamenei included praise for Iran's military forces, as well as for the former leader of the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon.

Khamenei was named Iran's new supreme leader soon after his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first round of U.S.-Israeli strikes, which sparked the war on Feb. 28.

The younger Khamenei has not been seen, even in video, since he was named the supreme leader, and senior U.S. officials have said he was likely seriously wounded in the same strike that killed his father.

Value of Iran's currency falls to all-time low against the dollar

The Iranian rial has fallen to a new historic low against the U.S. dollar, with the free-market selling rate surpassing 2.4 million rials per dollar on Monday.

Data from Pashizi, which tracks Iran's free-market exchange rates, put the dollar at around 2.4 million rials as Iran faces high inflation, sweeping sanctions and growing disruption to foreign trade.

Annual inflation has reached 61.4% in August, while food prices are reported to have risen 128% from a year earlier, according to data from Iran's Statistical Center .

Iran's U.N. delegation has no plans to negotiate directly with the U.S.

Iranian state media said Monday that Iran's delegation at the U.N. General Assembly in New York had no plans to hold direct talks with the U.S., after President Trump said he expected more negotiations to take place this week.

"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.

Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday he expected negotiations to continue this week, and added that the Iranian leaders were interested in reaching an agreement because they are "losing badly."

"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side... via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.

Since the outbreak of the war in February, negotiations between Tehran and Washington have occurred largely through mediators.

British police investigating possible Iranian links to suspected terrorist plot against U.K. air base used by U.S.

U.K. police said five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran were being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.

RAF Fairford, a U.K. Royal Air Force base about 85 miles west of London in rural Gloucestershire, has been used by American bombers to conduct strikes against Iranian missile sites. The British government, under an agreement made under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, granted the U.S. permission to use Farford and other key U.K. bases provided it was only for strikes defined as defensive in nature.

Authorities are investigating a link between the arrests in Fairford and Iran as one possibility. Iranian authorities have declared all bases used to attack Iranian territory as legitimate targets.

President Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests.

"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them."

Iran says it is ready for either diplomacy, or a return to fighting as war reaches 7-month mark

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready for either diplomacy or a return to fighting in the war sparked seven months ago by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. He said it is now up to President Trump to choose which direction to go.

"We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi told NBC News' "Meet the Press."

"At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he said.

President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to return to a ceasefire agreement that collapsed months ago as part of a seven-day plan that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.

Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.

Trump expects talks with Iran to resume this week

President Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, a day after he rejected a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.

"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."

Iran said Friday it had submitted a proposal to the U.S. to reopen the Strait of Hormuz over seven days, but Mr. Trump asserted that Iranian leaders wanted the deal because "they are losing so badly."

"They overplayed their hand," Mr. Trump told Axios.

The president said resuming strikes on Iran was not off the table, adding: "I am always thinking about it."
